speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-70, an Act to amend the Family Allowances Act, 1973, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on second reading of an Act to amend the Family Allowances Act, 1973. In the Budget of May 23, 1985, the Government, through the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), announced its intention to restructure the federal child benefit system to provide greater assistance to families with lower incomes while at the same time moving to bring our national debt under control. This Bill represents a first step toward meeting those dual objectives.
The major proposal contained in this Bill will modify the current method of indexing family and special allowances. Effective January, 1986, these benefits will be indexed only for the annual increase in the cost of living greater than 3 per cent. Any increase in inflation above 3 per cent will be fully compensated. I should also stress that, as is currently the case, no payment will be reduced if the rate of inflation drops from one year to the next. Thus, the principle of indexation will be maintained. Family allowances will continue to be protected by partial indexation should higher inflation occur. As well, Mr. Speaker, universality under that proposal is not affected.
Many of those concerned about the problem of the debt and the deficit advised a more drastic course of action. Indeed, there are those who advocated that government spending be reduced through the elimination of some of our social programs, and that includes family allowances.
Recently, the Macdonald Commission Report has advocated that current family benefits be eliminated above a certain income level as part of a guaranteed annual income proposal. The Government has chosen instead to maintain the principles of universality and indexation and to introduce a modification to the method of adjusting those benefits. In addition-and I cannot emphasize this enough-this represents a change to only one of the several components which make up the federal child benefit system. Over the next three years, the Government will be increasing the support currently provided to low income families through a gradual restructuring of benefits delivered through the tax system.
On second reading of this Bill, Mr. Speaker, I believe all of us in the House who have looked at the deficit, at Canada's economic status and at our public accounts, feel that it is important that the Government show a clear initiative in its approach to deficit restructuring. It is regrettable that this issue was not taken more seriously at an earlier date. The reason I say that is because one cannot separate, 1 would suggest, social programs and benefits from economic reality. I am sure Hon. Members opposite, as well as Hon. Members on this side of the House, do not endorse a system where today the servicing of the debt on an annualized basis is equal to the costs of services provided by the Department of National Health and Welfare. At the present time, the servicing of the debt on an annualized basis is approximately $26 billion. That is the budget for the Department of National Health and Welfare and of course, as Hon. Members know, it is the largest single budgetary item of any Department.
To put it in as succinct a term as I can, Mr. Speaker, the servicing of the debt today on an annual basis is equal to the federal Government's share of health care, of all old age pensions, of guaranteed income supplements for those Canadians who are below a certain income level, the spouses' allowance, the widows' allowance, the family allowance, welfare, social assistance for those who are most needy, medical research, and the list goes on. I believe Hon. Members realize that at any point in time Governments, regardless of their partisan stripe, like to see increases in social benefits. I do as well. But I also know that in order to maintain and improve those benefits, the deficit cannot be ignored by those of us who work in the social affairs field.
I want to serve notice to Hon. Members as well, that while this Bill amends the family allowances Act, although our legislative process does not allow for it, the follow-up legislation to improve child tax credit benefits are included in a Bill which the Minister of Finance will bring in. So while 1 am restricted to the Family Allowances Bill today, I remind Hon. Members of the total family benefits package when 1 am addressing this issue.
As Hon. Members know, the current child benefits system today is so irrationally structured that it actually provides greater after tax benefits to families with children and with an income of $30,000 than it does to a family with the same number of children and an income of $10,000. The revised system which we are proposing, and which will be in place by the end of 1989, will provide its maximum benefits to families with children and incomes of less than $25,000. Beyond that

September 16, 1985
Family Allowances Act
income level benefits will gradually diminish; but all families with children will continue to receive benefits not available to families without children with the same income.
[DOT] (mo)
While these groups have differed over mechanisms to reach such a structure, the initial level of benefits and the income level where benefits should begin to be reduced, all serious analysts of the current system have recommended reform based on the principles I have espoused. There must be more equity built into the system. At this point, I wish to thank the members of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs who also put forward a model. While we can argue models, I think the principles embodied are generally accepted from those in the social affairs field.
Such a system would also be markedly more progressive than the current one in the sense that a much larger portion of total benefits will flow to low income families with children while a smaller portion of total benefits will flow to upper income families with children. At the same time, as I have already stated, the universal character of the family allowances benefit is maintained.
Members opposite may wish to argue that the scheduled maximum benefit levels in the new system should be higher so that the number of winners compared to the current system would be increased. I wish to assure them that those levels will be reviewed on an ongoing basis and if fiscal conditions permit they may be increased in future Budgets.
I also want to remind the House that this is not the first time that limits have been placed on full indexing of the family allowance in conjunction with other changes to the child benefits system. When the child tax credit was introduced in 1979, the monthly family allowance was scheduled to increase from $25.68 per child to $27.99 per child. Instead, it was reduced to $20 per child. In 1983 and 1984, indexing of family allowances was limited to 6 per cent and 5 per cent by the so-called six and five program. Without that program, family allowances would have gone up from $26.91 per child per month in 1982 to $31.92 per child per month in 1984. Instead, the 1984 family allowance was $29.95 per child per month, almost $2 lower per month per child. To compensate, the child tax credit paid in 1983 and in 1984 was higher than it normally would have been before the restructure.
Further, it is also not the first time that less than full consumer price indexing has been applied as a restraint measure. In 1976, when the family allowance was scheduled to rise by 11.2 per cent, which was the inflation rate annualized at that time, from $22.08 per child per month to $24.55 per child per month, the Government of the day froze the level at the previous year's level. That is cost of living minus 11.2 per cent, not cost of living minus 3 per cent. There was no offsetting benefit increase in any other program in the child benefit system and the savings were fully applied to deficit reduction. I am sure my critic opposite in the Liberal Party remembers that period of time and the position taken.
I also suggest to the House that this restructuring is valid during a period of low inflation when inflation trends over the past number of years have been relatively stable. I think it is the right time, from that perspective as well, to make the adjustment. In fact, just looking back to 1976, if full indexing to the Consumer Price Index had been applied without interruption from 1974, the monthly family allowance cheque this year per child would be $51.83 instead of the current level of $31.27. That would be a difference of $20.56 per month, per child. I put these figures forward to convey to the House and the public that there have been changes along these lines before, much more dramatic, as I will point out later on, than anything we are suggesting in the Budget and in this Bill today. I say to the House and to every Canadian that there will not be a reduction in current levels, as was the case previously, but there will in fact be an increase. It will be less, however, than the CPI, namely 3 per cent less.
Given current levels of inflation this Bill will mean that the increase in family allowance benefits in 1986 will be 94 cents a month less per child than it would have been had the current system remained in place. I compare that 94 cents to the $20.56 which I am sure has not escaped the notice of the House. The comparable impact of the freeze in family allowances in 1976, to put it on a year-by-year basis because I think that is more accurate and more fair, in 1976 would have been $4.99 per month in 1985 dollars. To carry this argument even further, that would mean that in one year our model family with two dependants would have a total reduction of $22.72 for the entire year. What I am saying to Members is that we have to keep things in perspective. In addition we have the child tax credit for those in the lower income brackets which will be supplemented in further legislation. I point all this out not in a partisan manner but simply on the basis that it has been done before. I have no doubt that Members opposite will oppose this Bill, if their public announcements are to be believed, but I say to them that while it is their responsibility and obligation to oppose, they should do so in the light of history and oppose it in the light of what they did in the past.

They should oppose it in light of the deficit and in light of the arguments they made previously.
As is obvious from the points that I believe have been made today, Mr. Speaker, there is considerable precedent for what is being proposed in this Bill. I would now like to describe briefly the minor amendments to the family allowances program which are also included in the Bill and which I hope find acceptance with Members opposite. While these amendments are considered minor because they will not result in significant changes to the program, I believe they are none the less important because they serve to improve the equity and administration of the program on a day-by-day basis.
For example, one of the proposals would provide the Minister of National Health and Welfare with the discretionary

authority to remedy the consequences of erroneous advice given or administrative error made by departmental officials. 1 know from years of experience in opposition that we were always suspicious about giving a Minister discretionary powers.

However, I think as Members look at this proposal they will see it is to the benefit not of the Minister but of those who have suffered either from bad advice or clerical error. Given the substantial number of applicants and beneficiaries under the family allowances program, it is understandable that errors which result in a person or agency being denied an allowance may be made from time to time. While the Act does allow for retroactive payment of benefits of up to one year, cases may occur in which a loss of benefits extends beyond this retroactive period. If this amendment is approved, as I hope it will be, remedial action to rectify the consequences of erroneous advice or administrative error will be possible where it is demonstrated that a loss of benefit entitlement has occurred as a direct result of such errors.
Another proposal in the Bill would provide the Minister of National Health and Welfare with discretionary authority to remit or forgive an overpayment of family allowances under certain circumstances. Currently, in cases where it is determined that an overpayment of allowances has been made, the administration has no alternative under the terms of the Act but to proceed with the recovery of the overpayment, even though it might be excessively costly relative to the amount owed or take an unreasonable length of time to do so.
This amendment would give the Minister discretionary authority to remit benefit overpayments under these circumstances, as well as where the recovery of an overpayment would cause the debtor undue hardship or where the overpayment arose as a direct result of administrative error or erroneous advice on the part of a departmental official. I should say tangentially, Mr. Speaker, that this amendment would bring the Family Allowances Act in line with some other Acts relating to benefits paid under certain social programs.
One final amendment that has been included would authorize the Minister, where necessary, for the purposes of the Family Allowances Act, to issue a certificate declaring that a child is presumed to be dead. Unfortunately, we all know of tragic circumstances where a child disappears and there is sufficient evidence to presume that the child is dead. When this happens, the necessary benefit adjustments cannot be made until after a death certificate has been issued, sometimes many years after the child's disappearance. The proposed amendment would authorize the Minister, where the circumstances of the disappearance warrant it, to issue a certificate declaring that the child is presumed to be dead for the purposes of the Act and stating the date on which the death is presumed to have occurred. This will help families in terms of estate planning and so forth.
Family Allowances Act
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I believe this Bill merits the support of the House. It is part of a restructuring of the child benefits system which will ensure that the benefits given to families with children are distributed on a fairer and more rational basis. It will help improve the grave fiscal situation which faces us as a nation, and it will make the day-to-day administration of the Family Allowances Act more humane and flexible. Therefore, I move that this Bill be given second reading and referred to the appropriate committee.

Mr. Speaker, at the commencement of my remarks this morning I would like to indicate that the title of this Bill should be changed to "An Act to reflect Broken Promises and Lost Opportunities on behalf of the Conservative Government". I am glad to see that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) is going to remain in his seat and I trust that the members of his caucus will do the same in order that I can take them for a waltz down memory lane to remind them of some of the promises that the leading spokesman for their Party made during the months leading up to the election last September 4.
In November, 1983, the leading spokesman for that Party, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie), said, "If the Tories do monkey with the family allowance they would be able to do so only in their first year of power, and only if the public wanted to make more sacrifices". Three months later the present Minister of Justice said, "You have to be tough, mean, and nasty and do all kinds of unpleasant things. That's why I am not going to outline what they would do now, that's for a Government to do". How prophetic and truthful! He is one of one of the few spokesmen from the government front benches who told the truth before the election.
Let me remind Members opposite of some campaign promises made during the summer of the election of 1984. In August, 1984, their leader said:
Yes, I can give you the assurance that no social programs at all, affecting anyone in need shall be touched by a Progressive Conservative government. I can give you that without hesitation.

The Member opposite mentions the words "anyone in need". I am leading up to that in my premise. If he pays as much attention to the end of my speech as he did to my initial remarks, I will show him how people in need with family incomes of $9,000 a year will lose purchasing power as a result of his Conservative Budget. I will not even mention the Prime Minister's statement about sacred trust which he made a year ago. Let us consider the period immediately following the election of the Conservative Government. Last November 9, the Minister of Finance stated:
We feel there is a real opportunity here to put a greater degree of focus on those who need it most and still leave some money on the table that can be used for either deficit reduction or application in other ways to make a stronger economy.

Ten days later, in another interview, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that social benefits taxed back from the rich would be given to the needy if the federal government decides to end universality. The money would absolutely not be used to reduce the deficit.
What the Prime Minister said only 10 months ago is totally at loggerheads with what happened six months later in the budget of May 23.
What did the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) say at that time? In December, 1984, he rallied behind the Prime Minister's suggestion that the Government reduce social benefits for high income Canadians to help channel more to the poor. All of these promises contain the premise that if any of those benefits to our middle income or other sectors of our Canadian economy will be reduced, they will be channelled to those who need them the most.
In that same interview to UPC on December 14 last year, the Minister of National Health and Welfare said:
None of the saved benefits would reduce the deficit and there will be no means test.
I agree that there are no means tests, but when he suggests that as a result of the May 23 Budget the benefits would not be used to reduce the deficit, the facts belie the case.
Let me remind Members opposite of the other remarks they made about deindexation. For instance:
Deindexing is a scheme to guarantee that you will pay higher federal income taxes year after year after year.
They said:
Deindexing would take away the protection you now have against inflation.
I will reveal who made these quotes later. They went on to say that deindexing would impose the greatest economic hardship on people living on low income and would mean higher and higher taxes for all on any income at all. They said that taxes would increase as inflation continues to spiral upward.
They also went on to point out that deindexing would raise a lot of money. I will point out the truth of that fact as I analyse the budget numbers.
They also said:
Indexing was our idea in the first place. And we are determined that you should continue to receive this fundamental protection against inflation. But we need your help and it is time for all Canadians to speak up.
This was not taken from an advertisement run by the Liberal Party of Canada. It is contained in a message from the Progressive Conservative Party of Canda, published midway through the last mandate.
Let me put some of these promises in the context of what I want to say this morning. I noticed that the Minister of National Health and Welfare selectively quoted from the MacDonald Commission Report.

However, my remarks this morning will take into consideration some of the recommendations made by the MacDonald Commission and other national organizations that report to the Minister of National Health and Welfare and with advice about what the Government's social policy should be.
The McDonald Report contends that Canada's total level of spending on social programs, which, in 1981, was in the lower one-third of countries belonging to the Organization for Cooperation and Development, should at least be maintained. The commission also declared that it does not fear for the future sustainability of our income transfer programs. Nor does it believe that short-time budgetary problems should be solved through cut-backs in this area, something totally opposite to the thrust of the social and economic policy of the Wilson Budget of May 23.
Let me talk a little bit about the Budget. I notice that the Minister of National Health and Welfare chose only to address those matters specifically within the realm of Bill C-70, but I think the general thrust of the budget measures should be taken into account. Once again, opposition Members of this Parliament will have to rise to defend average and low-income Canadians. We went through a similar debate in June with respect to deindexation of senior citizens pensions. I must say I am proud that we helped to lead the fight to reverse the Government's thrust in that area, and 1 give credit to the Government for its common sense in listening to senior citizens. I hope the Government listens equally well to those average income and low-income Canadians, and reverses the measures placed before us in Bill C-70.
Let us look at the proposals in the Budget and what effect they will have on total family income. This summer we have heard from women's groups and national organizations that represent poverty groups, the National Council on Social Development and the National Council on Welfare, all of which state that this Government's social policy is perverse and totally opposite to what is required to give poor people a reasonable good standard of living.
This Government has chosen to introduce capital gains exemptions for the rich in our society. I have no quarrel with some of the other recommendations, for example, limits on registered retirement savings plans. But the Government has chosen not only to deindex family benefits but to deindex personal exemptions. This means that every family by 1990 whether earning $9,000, $35,000 or $80,000 a year will lose purchasing power. That is the reality. This is the Budget in which the multinationals will get significant taxbreaks. If we were worried about the size of the federal deficit, why is it that we have cut-backs in social programs yet allow these kinds of rip-offs to occur that add to the size of the federal deficit?
That is the question at the heart of the debate today, Mr. Speaker. Bill C-70 is another example of broken Tory promises. Let me give a short outline. Both Mulroney and Epp promised that any savings in social spending would go back into the social policy envelope, not on deficit reduction.

It is very simple to me. The Minister of Finance is quite capable of finding $1 billion to bail out the Canadian Commercial Bank while sticking by his decision to cut back in areas of the social envelope.
What did we get specifically in this Budget? We ended up with an erosion in family benefits, meaning less benefits by 1990 to low and middle-income Canadians. The Budget will increase consumer and gasoline taxes. The Budget will impose taxes on health goods. We had a Budget that attempted to deindex senior citizens' security pensions, but was withdrawn under fierce opposition. We have a Budget that will deindex personal income tax exemption. These changes will hit lower income Canadians the hardest. All low-income Canadians will have to pay income tax and lose a proportion of their family allowance gain while the richest Canadians will benefit from the capital gains exemption.
I will give numbers from an analysis done by an independent board of advisers to the Minister of National health and Welfare. These numbers cannot be disputed because they were accepted by the Finance Minister in questions put to him in the House of Commons last June. The analysis shows that the Government's direction in social policy is completely at odds with policy directions recommended by all national organizations advising Government.
I find it perverse that a Government wanting to stimulate the Canadian economy and get growth at the same rate as that south of the border would choose to bring in a Budget eroding the spending power of lower and middle-income Canadians. This Budget will make the poor poorer and the rich richer, yet the Government expects Canadians to have the political will to follow its general thrust. This Budget has broad fiscal overtones completely opposed to those in the United States.
We have many Conservatives pointing to the economic recovery program south of the border. Great growth has occurred in the United States in the last four years. At the same time, great growth in the deficit has occurred. If one wants to analyse it, one could say, in a reverse, despite the fact that President Reagan would never admit it-I do not think he would even understand-that he has been more of a follower of Keynes economic theory than any United States President since Roosevelt.
In order to achieve growth the Americans granted average income Americans tax cuts and increased taxes for big corporations. That was the general over-all fiscal policy of the United States Government in the last four years, completely opposite to what was brought in here in the May 23 Budget.
Let me outline numbers and give specifics. We had a decrease in purchasing power to average and low-income Canadians. We have had income tax increases and corporate
Family Allowances Act
tax cuts. Specifically, families with two children and an income of $20,000 a year will lose over $900 in spending power by 1990, through eroded child benefits, increased consumptive taxes and increased income taxes.
Talking about perverse social logic, Mr. Speaker, as a result of the Budget on May 23, three-quarters of a million Canadians who are presently above Stats-Canada's poverty line will fall below that poverty line by 1990. In addition, let us take another area of thrust with respect to young families. In the Budget of May 23, the Minister removed the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan, a tool used by young people, 75 per cent of whom are between the ages of 20 and 28. No longer can young families put aside money toward buying a home through the RHOSP.
Let us examine some of the fundamental philosophy behind the introduction of family allowances by previous Governments. First, it was recognized that the family allowance is a tangible recognition that all parents make a contribution to society by raising children who are future citizens and members of the labour force. It is an especially significant program for women. That is why women's groups defend the family allowance so vigorously. Even for more affluent families it is often the only independent source of income for women in cases where husbands refuse to provide their wives and their children with income.
Let us take a look at the importance to single parent mother-lead families of family allowances. Family benefits have an important role in supplementing incomes for poor families. It also compensates for the fact that the wage system does not make adjustments for the extra responsibility of large families. That was at the heart of the philosophy behind the introduction of family benefits in previous years. Needless to say, family benefits stimulate the economy by putting purchasing power into the hands of low and middle-income Canadians. That ends my review of the over-all general thrust of the Conservative Budget of May 23, 1985.

I should now like to focus for a moment on some of the specifics as a result of the changes in Bill C-70. It is indicated that the family allowance will be deindexed from 1986 onward. The child tax credit will be raised to $454 per child in 1986, rising to $489 in 1987 and peaking at $524 in 1988. The Minister of National Health and Welfare refused to recognize in his opening remarks that beginning in 1989 the child tax credit would be deindexed along with the other proposals. As a result of the deindexation of the child tax credit, even those who will receive an initial benefit from the program change, those who are the poorest of the poor, will receive that increased benefit only from 1986 to 1989. In 1989 and beyond, even a family, God forbid, living on $9,000 per year will lose benefits under the program. What kind of perverse social policy are the back-benchers of the Conservative Party supporting? That is the effect of that one item.
In addition, the Minister of National Health and Welfare conveniently overlooked, in terms of the recommendations

September 16, 1985
Family Allowances Act
made by his own standing committee, the turning point or the point at which middle income Canadians begin to lose benefits. The effect of Bill C-70 is that the turnover point will be lowered from $26,333 today to $23,500 tomorrow, and then it will even be partially deindexed. Even the definition of Statistics Canada of medium family income is $34,500. In effect the Government is suggesting through this Bill that families at $26,000 per year should lose benefits. It is incredible that the Government would consider that the average Inco worker in Sudbury, the average steelworker in Hamilton or the average worker in Thunder Bay should begin to lose benefits under the family benefits package. That tells me everything about 14 years of Tory think-tanks on social policy. A combination of all these changes will cause lower and middle-income Canadian families to be hit the hardest.
Let us take a look at the effects on Canadian families. By 1990, including the changes to personal income taxes and to the family benefits package, a two-earner, two-child family earning $15,000 per year will lose $1,879 in purchasing power as a result of the Bill. A family earning $80,000, or almost six times the amount which I just mentioned, will only lose $1,125. Therefore, low-income families will lose $755 more per year than high-income families, and middle-income families will lose three times as much as high-income earners. What kind of perverse logic leads a Government to bring in such a Bill? At the same time, the capital gains exemption and pension deductions mainly benefit high-income earners. As a result of the capital gains exemption, those with incomes of over $100,000 per year will receive more than $600 million in tax benefits, while changes to the Child Tax Credit and the child tax exemption will save the Government only $155 million. If we take the Minister of National Health and Welfare at his word when he indicates that he is worried about the size of the federal deficit, how can he, in defending the rights of low and middle-income earners, sit around a Cabinet table which brings in a Budget to make the rich richer and the poor poorer? It is beyond belief.
As I stated earlier, the savings of the Government will go toward deficit reduction. It will not go back into the social policy envelope, as was recommended by every national advisory group. This Government prided itself in consultation. It said that the reason for the 10-month delay in the introduction of the Budget was to ensure proper consultation with all groups in society. Every one of those groups recommended the total opposite to what was brought in. What was the point of the charade of consultation if the advice given was not taken?
What do groups at arms length from Government have to say about the over-all thrust of the Conservative Budget and this Bill in particular? The Canadian Council on Social Development, funded by the federal Government, has been giving advice to the Government of the nation for years. It indicated that the Budget would decrease the buying power of a typical family with two children by more than $1,000 in 1990. It went on to point out that the poor, middle-income earners and the elderly would lose more as a percentage of income in real
terms. Let us note, in particular, the economic thrust and direction of the Budget.
Instead of confusing everyone by using figures such as $4.50 per month and by talking about individuals, I should like to talk about what happens to the percentage of disposable income of Canadians as a result of the budgetary measures of May 23. A family earning a gross income of $10,000 will lose 4 per cent of disposable income by 1990, whereas a family earning $20,000 will lose 4.5 per cent of disposable income. However, the family earning $50,000 will gain .7 per cent. As a result of this budget exercise, a family earning $10,000 per year will lose 4 per cent of disposable income and a family earning $50,000 per year will gain almost 1 per cent.
How can the Conservatives rise in the House of Commons and tell us that the Budget will help to redirect savings toward those who need them the most when it goes totally opposite to the direction intended? If that is the case, the least they can do is bring in a Bill which reverses the direction of May 23. As a result of deindexation, by 1990 the Government will gain $4.5 billion. It managed to give to the multinationals $2 billion worth of tax credits as a result of the changes to the National Energy Program. At a time when it proposes to take away $2 billion by 1990 from health and post-secondary education, it gives away $1.5 billion on capital gains exemption. That will be the cost to the federal Treasury. The effect of the Budget on the social and economic sectors of the economy will be totally opposite to that put forward by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare. If one looks at the deficit reduction and at where the moneys for that deficit reduction will come from through tax increases and expenditure cuts, primarily it will be achieved- and this is no surprise-in the social sectors. As a matter of fact, collectively the deindexation of income tax, the removal of the federal tax deduction and the changes to the child benefits system will account for almost $5.5 billion of that cut. If we look at the over-all thrust of the Budget, the big gains will be made in the area of corporate income tax, by multinational oil companies, and in the area of transfers to other corporations. The lack of logic of the Government in bringing in this Budget is incredible. The National Council on Welfare indicated that the recommendations in Bill C-70 and in the Budget would hurt many low-income families and individials in all age groups. It went on to indicate that their losses would amount to hundreds of dollars per year and would grow larger as time went on. In addition, it went on to explain how proposed changes to the personal income tax system would increase the tax bill of lower and middle-income Canadians and would actually lighten the tax burden of many upper-income taxpayers. It pointed out that a two-earner couple supporting two children on $15,000 per year would pay $135 more in federal and provincial income taxes next year, that the same size of family with a combined income of $35,000 would pay a $192 increase in taxes, but that an $80,000 per year family would actually enjoy a tax saving of $650 per year.
September 16, 1985

So what hypocrisy it is to stand and tell me, as a Conservative Government, that the thrust of your Government is to try to get more money into the hands of those who need it most!
All other families, Mr. Speaker, including many below the poverty line, will lose child benefits from 1986 onward if the Budget's proposals are implemented. I cannot stress enough the hypocrisy of this Government in these recommendations.
What did the Canadian Council on Children and Youth have to say about this Budget, Mr. Speaker? In pre-Budget consultations with the Government, here is what it recommended: preserve the universality of the family allowances and as a tax benefit-the Government listened to it-eliminate the child tax exemption partially; raise the child tax credit for low-income families partially; raise the threshold at which child tax credit is recaptured. To the last one the Government did not listen at all. Here is what the Government ended up doing. It deindexed the family allowances. It reduced the child tax exemption by 34 per cent over three years and subject to deindexation. It increased the child tax credit by 140 over three years but chose to deindex it after 1988, which means even the poorest of the poor will lose under this proposal beginning in 1990. It indicated that middle-income families will be the hardest hit and bear the brunt of these changes.
I just want to talk a bit about what we believe, as the Liberal Party, should be the principles inherent as a guide to the creation of a new child benefit system.
First, we believe that universality of family allowances should be maintained; second, low-income earners should receive more than those in the upper-income brackets; and higher benefits should be paid to lower-income families. That is a policy direction that we believe in. We believe that indexation should be maintained and that family benefits should be adjusted to reflect changes in the cost of living.
Last but not least, and most important, the sharing of the cost of these universal programs should be borne and shared by all taxpayers, corporate and individuals, through a fair taxation system. That is inherent in this. In addition, Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the Conservative Government is not taking the recommendations of the OECD surveys, or the Macdonald Report which raised this issue previously, that the percentage of dollars of the federal Budget that is going towards, those areas that are reflected in social policy envelopes should be increased.
I want to indicate, Mr. Speaker, as well, that the Liberal Party over the next weeks and months ahead will be launching an operation called Operation Justice. I do not know if the Minister of National Health and Welfare remembers that we launched a similar program in June to convince the Government about the unfairness of the plan to deindex senior citizens pensions.
We are asking, Mr. Speaker, all the senior citizens groups in this country to help to get the people's opposition to this plan to change family benefits read into the record and brought
Family Allowances Act
back forcefully to every one of the MPs as they go home to their own ridings.
I point out as well that the middle class is especially hard hit by the Budget in this Operation Justice and requests help from not only the groups that represent the poor in our society, but from Members of Parliament, the Conservative Members of Parliament, who have an obligation, to bring forward the viewpoints of middle-income and low-income Canadians to the floor of the House of Commons and not sit back and clap like seals as the Government brings in a program that is going to devastate low and middle-income Canadians.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, I want to move the following motion as follows;
That the main motion be amended deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting therefor:
Bill C-70, an Act to amend the Family Allowances Act, 1973, be not now
read a second time but that it be read a second time this day six months hence.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I rise really with a feeling of sadness to speak to Bill C-70 because, jsut as we feel that the Budget had such a sad impact on families and pensioners in our country, this Bill certainly symbolizes once again how this Government really is prepared to conduct an attack on children and families as well as to allow an erosion of our universal programs. Canadians have seen the erosion of social programs such as the family allowance which is a social contract with them establishing rights for children, regardless of income.
I think we all recall, Mr. Speaker, last spring when pensioners across this country rose up in indignation and anger to demand their right to have fully indexed pensions. They, of course, mobilized considerable support across the country. Many of us went out to work with them in this very important endeavour and, as a result, they were able to convince the Government that it had made a mistake. Pensioners convinced the Government politically; I'm not sure, when I see this Bill, that they convinced it morally that it had made a mistake when it proposed to deindex a universal social program.
As a result of the campaign we know now, it is history, that the Government was forced to back down and to admit that it was wrong. After a protracted attack from both opposition parties, but particularly from the NDP Party, senior groups and their supporters across this country, the decision was reversed. Fully indexed old age pensions were retained as a universal right. I disagree profoundly with the Minister and I think we need to stress very strongly, Mr. Speaker, that to deindex old age pensions or family allowances is to play around with the whole concept of universality and to erode
6626

September 16, 1985
Family Allowances Act
that concept. That is what we are doing to family allowances through Bill C-70.
Mr. Speaker, the polls show that this Government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was left with a legacy of mistrust and skepticism as a result of his broken promises, and what he proposed to do to senior citizens.
Now we have Bill C-70, a Bill which in effect will do the same thing to families and children. It will reduce the indexation on family allowance by 3 per cent and is repeating the same cynical and senseless attack on a universal social program, a program which Canadians have long seen as a social right. The same principles and objections apply to the reduced indexation on family allowances as apply to old age pensions, so therefore the Government should be listening to people and applying the same kinds of changes in policy as were applied to pensions in the spring. They promised, as we know, Mr. Speaker, to keep universality sacrosanct, that it was a sacred trust, and then they have broken their promises once again. This time, of course, the attack is on families and children. I cannot help but think that it is much easier to attack children than it is to attack old age pensioners. Children do not vote; their parents are busy working and the children grow up very quickly. The amount of money expended for the Family Allowances Program is not as large as that expended for the Old Age Security Program. Therefore, that is another reason why I think it would have been sensible and morally responsible of the Minister to have changed this intention that was reflected in the Budget and to have refused to deindex family allowances.
The Government continues its practice of saying one thing and doing another. This Minister of National Health and Welfare is the epitome of this. He really symbolizes this to the greatest extent of anyone in the Government, except perhaps for the Prime Minister. On repeated occasions, and again last week in the House, he has said that he has a very strong commitment to the importance of the family. I just want to quote what he said on September 11 in a response to a question from one of the opposition Members. He said:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the Hon. Member has recognized the importance that both the Government and Canadian society place on the family unit. 1 think many of us in this House and in society generally feel that that concept had to be strengthened, that there were certain trends in society that were possibly reducing the importance of the family.
Listen to this, Mr. Speaker:
This Government wants to bring forward initiatives that will enhance both the Government's position relative to the family, but more important, show that the family is the cornerstone of society.
The Minister is saying that the family is so important while he is introducing Bill C-70, a Bill which attacks all families, not only one segment of society. He is attacking a universal program and he has the gall to put forward in his patronizing manner the point that he cares about families, that they are the basis of his social policy and that he is particularly concerned about those in greatest need. I cannot help but conclude, and I believe most Canadians would conclude, that
just as the Government's policy with pensioners was hypocritical, the same can be said about the family allowance policy.
As I said, the Minister has repeated that the Government is concerned with helping those in greatest need. That is just phoney rhetoric. The facts show that the Conservative Budget represents an attack on the poorest families in our society while rich families continue to benefit. I will elaborate on this further later in my remarks.
The reduction to the family allowance which this Bill implements is only one of the ways in which the Government is undermining families and children. Added to the erosion of family allowances in the lowering of the income limit to be eligible for the child tax credit. The token increase in the child tax credit over whith the Minister tends to gloat does not even cover the increased sales taxes that those same poor families will be forced to pay. The sales taxes on gas, energy products, health products and comforts contained in the last Budget will cost the average family over $1,000 in buying power by 1990 according to the Canadian Council on Social Development.
I would like to point out to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) that he is the Minister who is responsible for health. He has supported taxes on essential drugs and medications for patients suffering from arthritis, cancer, glaucoma and heart disease. This again is the way that he is treating those in greatest need and those in our society who are suffering. In contrast to that, we know how the Government treats the banks and the oil companies.
The Minister, who seems to be amused by this particular approach, has taken the initiative to reduce other services to families. He has cut services to Planned Parenthood at the very time when we need these services to be enlarged across the country, particularly in order to help young adolescents, a group among whom there is a very high incidence of pregnancy. There are cuts in social housing. Rents are going up to 30 per cent of income and responsibility for social housing will apparently be turned over to the provinces. We in British Columbia know what that will do to families.
As well, the Government has decreased transfer payments to provinces for health care and education services by $2 billion. This will also have a tremendous impact on families and will hurt families in which the breadwinner is unemployed, poor families and marginal families in which the breadwinner is struggling to find a job, take training or maintain the health of the family.
Some months ago, the Minister asked for consultation. Then he assigned the Standing Committee on Health and Welfare to the task of looking at some of the consultation papers and briefs that had been presented by witnesses. As the Hon. Member who just spoke will confirm, we spent weeks and weeks doing this. Both the recommendations of witnesses and the recommendations of the Standing Committee on Health and Welfare were in effect ignored by the Minister. It is obvious that his motivation and that of the Government was to cut family benefits in order to save money rather than to reform benefits in a very progressive way.
September 16, 1985

In his Blue Paper to the Standing Committee, the Minister stated that savings from the changes to family benefits would not be aimed at reducing the deficit. Yet today, if I understood him correctly, he admitted in his opening remarks that that was one of the objectives of this program.
Most witnesses who appeared before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs advocated full indexation of family allowances and the maintaining of universal family programs which recognize all of Canada's children. They also supported the position, which we advocated very strongly, that all citizens of Canada should contribute to the cost of programs for Canada's children as they are a resource that belongs to all of us, not only to the parents who are raising individual children. Most witnesses therefore asked for full indexation of family allowances and wanted a removal of the regressive child tax exemption, a tax provision that progressively helps those with higher incomes and does not help in the slightest poor families that pay no taxes. They also wanted to see a significant increase in the child tax credit. Our Party called for an increase of 80 per cent in the child tax credit if the child tax exemption could be removed and other tax reforms instituted to cover this. This measure would be targeted particularly to lower income people but should also affect families with average incomes, families that have higher expenses than families without children.
The witnesses urged that all monies should go to increased family benefits and not go toward other social programs or the deficit. They urged particularly that there not be a transfer of any savings to the provinces. The Minister has completely ignored almost all of these recommendations. He has taken a completely different tack. Instead of being a reform, this legislation is a token juggling around which adds up to a very negative change as it affects most families.
In addition to reducing indexation on both the family allowance and the child tax credit, the Government has agreed to cut the child tax exemption after several years, but the exemption will only be cut partially. It will not be removed as was advocated by most witnesses. It will go down to about the same level as the family allowance. The child tax credit will have only a token increase of $70 this year, but more than that amount of money will be required by families to pay the increased sales taxes. The income level at which families will be eligible for the child tax credit has also been reduced. Families that earn over $23,500 per year will quickly be phased out of eligibility for the child tax credit.
Over-all, we have a situation in which wealthier families retain tax exemptions for children, the poor have only token increases in the child tax credit along with heavier expenses as a result of the Budget, and middle-income families, as usual, will pay the most taxes and reap the least benefits in proportion to the taxes paid. However, let us take a look at who really benefits as a result of changes and modifications to the family benefits.
Despite the promise not to take monies out of the family benefits to pay for the deficit, the Government will save approximately $130 million in 1986 and up to $600 million by
Family Allowances Act
1990 while families will lose this amount of money in direct family benefits. If this is not a contradiction of the original philosophy that the Minister, in his patronizing manner, was espousing, I do not know what is. I wish he would own up to that. This is the way the Minister of National Health and Welfare is treating families, families which, as he says, are the foundation of our society. This is the way he helps families that are most in need.
The Canadian Council on Social Development did an analysis of the impact of a 3 per cent reduction in indexation of family allowances combined with the other changes to family benefits which the Budget will implement. It definitely refutes the Minister's claim that he is helping families in the greatest need. The CCSD concludes that all families will be the losers of family benefits by the years 1990-91. Even the very poorest family, that is, a single parent with two children who earns under $10,000 a year, will lose under these revisions. By 1990, this family will receive $25 less per year than it receives now, while the Minister extols the fact that he is giving more to the poor. The CCSD says that that is not true, that its facts show he will be giving less. Families in the $20,000 income range will lose $191 in family benefits. Those earning $30,000, which is still a modest income for a family with two children, will have family benefits reduced by $191. Clearly, the Budget did not redistribute benefits from the rich to poor families at all. In fact, what this Government has done is to take money out of family benefits altogether. As I have just said, this must have been the motive. I think the Minister admitted to that today, even though in his position papers he stated this was not to be the objective. The Government has definitely been taking money out of the program to help with the deficit. This also applies to the provinces which will save money off the backs of families. According to the CCSD, $135 million will be withdrawn from family benefits by 1986; by 1990-91, some $600 million will be lost to Canada's children. As 1 have said, the provincial and federal Treasuries will be the beneficiaries of this money.
The New Democratic Party is not the only group to criticize the 3 per cent reduction in family allowance which Bill C-70 proposes to implement. Most social policy groups and women's groups across Canada have been highly critical and they are becoming very disillusioned. Most of these groups made a sincere attempt to present positive, realistic alternatives which would not cost the Government a great deal of money but, instead, would realign existing moneys. The six groups which now form part of the Social Policy Reform Group, which is a coalition of social reform groups, tried to present alternatives in a sincere and constructive manner. These groups are now disillusioned by the tack the Minister has taken. The Executive Director of the Canadian Council on Social Development had this to say with respect to the matter:
Changes to child benefits affect the very programs that help the neediest Canadians.

September 16, 1985
Family Allowances Act
This is what the National Council on Welfare had to say:
Changes in the Budget to deindex those benefits, coupled with increases to personal income taxes, will result in more hardship to the poor, who will eventually lose more than the rich.
The Director of the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, Sylvia Gold, said:
The economic security of women with children at home is threatened by deindexation of family allowances and the child tax credit. We strenuously object to this chipping away of family benefits; these cuts may not seem major to high income people, but they will have a serious effect on families with moderate and low incomes.
I wish to tell Hon. Members that I have contact with many women's groups across the country. They strongly oppose any reduction to family allowance benefits. This is an attack on their children and an attack on them. It is an attack which is not to be tolerated. I hope they will be able to get their message across loud and clear to the Minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) with respect to how damaging this policy is. It is a policy which is a continuation of a process which the Liberals started. I agree with what the Minister had to say in his outline of the Liberal history. However, I do not know how he can justify his comments when, on the one hand, he criticizes the Liberals and, on the other hand, he says that his Government is bad, too-just not quite as bad. I think the Minister is worse because he is continuing the erosion and not reversing it. It is hurting families and children across our land.
The purpose and effects of Bill C-70 are far more significant than just the 3 per cent reduction in family allowance. Perhaps this will not be noticed by a great many people, particularly fairly comfortable families. However, I can tell Hon. Members it will be noticed by families which are budgeting hard and simply do not have money in their budgets or their pockets to cover food and rent. What this move represents is an attack on the whole concept of the universal family program which was designed by our forefathers to help in the rearing of Canada's children and which was designed to recognize all of Canada's children.
As 1 have said, the Liberals began the process of reducing the amount of family allowance. They are to blame. I challenge the member of the Liberal Party who just spoke to be more honest in his self-appraisal. The Liberals refused to make a truly effective program with a more progressive tax system to go along with it which would have targeted benefits of a universal program to those in low income groups. Instead, they reduced the family allowance. They added a selective program, the child tax credit, for low income families and they changed the tax system so that, in fact, higher income earners received more benefits and more exemptions. The implementation of selective programs allowed them to ignore the need for tax reform. They further eroded the universal family allowance by imposing six and five restrictions on indexation in 1984. This was the beginning of the precedent which helps to justify the measures being taken by the Conservative Government with respect to Bill C-70. It is unethical and damaging. In my view, it is abominable.
I wish to reiterate what I have said many times in the House on different occasions. I think it is important to repeat it. Why
is it important to maintain a fully indexed universal family allowance? The universal family allowance recognizes the value which society places on child rearing. It is not just an amount of money; it is recognition of the fact that children belong to us all. They are the next generation; they are a human resource. Parents who take on the sometimes difficult and costly job of rearing children should be recognized.
The universal family allowance program contributes to parenting and to the costs of child rearing. I greatly admire the contribution made by the women of this country and 1 hope that, increasingly, fathers can be included in the realm of child rearing full-time.
Mir. McDermid: That is a sexist statement.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
It is not a sexist remark at all, Mr. Speaker. 1 hope more fathers will take time off to help in the rearing of their children full-time when it is suited to the families. Parenting should be a shared responsibility.
The fact is that family allowances are paid for by all taxpayers. This is the means by which those of us who do not have children contribute to the next generation.
The family allowance is paid to the main parenting person, which could be the father. However, because of circumstances, it is usually the mother. As has already been stated, for many women this is the only cheque they receive in their own names. This morning I was on the red eye special in order to be on time for this momentous meeting of the House. 1 had the opportunity of speaking to two men on the plane. I was interested in one gentleman who is an accountant who told me that he thought the family allowance was great. He asked me why it went to his wife when he is the one who has to pay the taxes on it. I asked him if his wife had any form of income, and he told me that she did not. He soon realized that the family allowance cheque was the only income his wife had in her name, even though he had a considerable income. He also realized that the funds went to his children in the form of clothing allowances. He thinks it is very much needed. He did not want to give up the family allowance even though he himself is in fairly comfortable circumstances. He recounted to me the struggles he had in his student years and how the money was needed even more at that time. It is really small recognition for the many long hours, love and stress which go into parenting. Some mothers who are working use the money to help pay for the cost of child care. We need more help for child care in the country. Parents on average incomes use it to help buy costly winter coats and clothing and to help cover schooling costs and other activities which help their children to grow up and mature with a broad range of interests.
Poor mothers and poor families, of course, are the most desperate. I want to tell those Hon. Members who are heckling across the way that I hope they have talked to some mothers who are on welfare these days, because in my riding, I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, it is no laughing matter. Mothers have a welfare cheque which lasts about two weeks, if they are lucky,
September 16, 1985

and that is with absolutely no comforts of any kind. It is just basic food, rent and transportation. By the third week they are down at food banks trying to get money. They are desperate for their family allowance cheque which immediately goes for either rent or food. By the fourth week some of them are out soliciting on the streets because they cannot afford to feed their families. That is how bad it is. And we are taking the indexation off their family allowance cheque as well as providing insulting kinds of increases to the child tax credit which should have been much higher.
Another thing which I believe is important about the family allowances is that the cheque comes on a monthly basis. Low income families also very much appreciate the fact that the child tax credit is an additional bonus on an annual basis. They like it as a larger amount, according to the national anti-poverty group, because it is the only way they can pay for certain larger household items. We must remember, Mr. Speaker, that poor families and families on welfare have no access to credit whatsoever and have to pay top prices for all their consumer goods.
I would like to say as well, Mr. Speaker, that it is important that the family allowance and old age pensions remain universal programs because they are paid out to everyone as a right. There is no stigma and no need for a huge bureaucracy to deal with individual cases through a means test. It is declared on income tax forms and partially recovered from those on higher incomes. The family allowance is especially important because it is one of the few benefits which go to middle income earners who carry the greatest tax burden to pay for our social programs.
These programs are also important politically. I would urge the Minister to think of that as well because he is going to get lots of backlash from the middle class in Canada-it has started already-who realize that they are the ones who are paying more the costs of all of the items in the Budget as well as the deficit and they, in turn, are going to have their one small benefit, the family allowance, made smaller by reduced indexation. So a very important political factor is involved in maintaining support for our universal social programs.
A fully indexed family allowance is a basic component of our Canadian social policy. Parents feel that this is their social right to which they are contributing by raising Canada's children. And they are right. It is a social contract we have with families just as we have with old age pensioners. This is the same principle as that of the universal old age pensions. We are very proud of our social security system in Canada which Hon. Members of our Party fought for and pressured the Liberals to bring in in the early 1930s. We are proud of our medicare, our hospitalization plan, our public educational system and our Unemployment Insurance Act, just as we are proud of universal family allowances and old age security. These are programs which this Government seems intent to erode, and this Minister, particularly, has no conscience about deindexing. This kind of partial deindexation now is just the first step, Mr. Speaker. There is no question in my mind that it
Family Allowances Act
is a first step which will eventually lead to the erosion of our social net if we do not protest and stop it now.
I must deplore the fact that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is advocating a 3 per cent deindexation while he says over and over again-he said it again today-that he supports universality. I am sick and tired of those platitudes. He says he supports universality and this is not in any way eroding our universal family program. That is ridiculous. It is eroding it. It is reducing the amount of money which will go into the pockets of low income families and every year it will be reduced even more. If that is not reducing universality, I do not know what is.
The Minister's lack of support for universality, I might say, is also reflected in statements he made in reaction to the Macdonald Commission Report, which recently advocated a guaranteed annual income, which really should be called "a guaranteed poverty income", because that is exactly what it is.
I do not have time to go into this today, Mr. Speaker, but I hope we will debate this report at another time.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare, according to The Citizen of September 7, hinted he may be prepared to reopen the debate on the universality of social programs after carefully considering the recommendation of the Macdonald Commission. That report, as 1 understand it, does away with universal programs and offers a guaranteed income, which would be guaranteed poverty because it is a fraction of what the minimum poverty rate is in Canada. I feel that that is a pretty shocking kind of statement and I wish the Minister would elaborate on what he meant by saying he would be inclined to support the Macdonald Commission proposals. The decision to deindex family allowances really must be seen in the context not only of broader family benefits-and that is what I have been trying to do today-but also in the context of the need for social policy reform generally. We need real reforms of social policy as it affects families. This kind of piecemeal approach which chips away at its benefits is really detrimental.
Changes in social policy must address the changing needs of today's families with children. I believe we have to look at the whole concept of families today. Families have changed so much and our social policy is not adapting to the different circumstances. Canadians have long recognized that incomes from the market-place failed to take into account the extra responsibilities shouldered by parents. Through tax provisions and family allowances we have taken steps to ensure that families with children do not have to endure a significantly lower standard of living than their childless counterparts. Changing demographics and work patterns make these concerns even more pressing today. I mentioned the number of teenage mothers in society today, and I think the Minister should be not only providing them with adequate incomes but should be trying to prevent, through support for family planning, that very real problem.
Social policy should also address the growing needs of the poor who now number 4.5 million Canadians. This includes 1.5 million children. While one in every six Canadians lives in

September 16, 1985
Family Allowances Act
poverty, the figure for children under 16 is one in five. There are a million and a half people unemployed, according to the figures we had last spring and, certainly in my province, I would be very surprised if that figure has fallen from that. Real family incomes are falling. Salaries still trail inflation rates. Most unions, I believe, would agree with that because of what they have lost over the last few years. Soup kitchens and winter clothing drives are becoming the norm across Canada. Recently, a report of the Anglican Church of Canada, accused both the federal and provincial Governments of shirking their responsibilities by relying on churches and volunteer organizations to feed, clothe and shelter the needy. What we need are sound social policies.
I feel that the kind of trivial remarks which are being made by Hon. Members opposite are really doing a disservice to both churches and poor people, Mr. Speaker.
As the author of the report of the Anglican Church of Canada said:
The State's failure to provide an adequate social support system has widened the gap between the poor and the privileged, plunging the country into another
depression.
The number of poor people rose by 1,100 a day in 1982 and 1983. So we must think of social policy reform, Mr. Speaker, in the context of over-all tax reform. The two are tightly entwined. This is why we regret that the Conservatives refused to talk about tax reforms. We wanted major reforms in the tax system so that we could be more generous, particularly in increasing the child tax credit and maintaining fully indexed family allowances. We proposed several ways of gaining extra income: A return to the pre-1982 marginal tax rates which would have brought in $1.7 billion more and which the Liberals foolhardedly left in the coffers under MacEachen's Budget; the imposition of a 20 per cent minimum tax on Canadians with incomes of $50,000 per year or more. The Prime Minister promised to do something about this we have seen no action. Once again we get words and platitudes but no action.
I want to conclude by saying that we call on Canadians across this land, from all walks of life, to tell this Government that they stand for fully indexed family allowances. It is not simply family allowances by themselves. It is really a basic family benefit program which should be reformed to be of much greater benefit to middle and low income Canadians. I call on those people to begin the fight for reindexation of family allowances just as they fought for reindexation of old age pensions. It is the same principle, the same fight, and I know in my heart from talking to seniors across the land that they care just as much about children as they care about their retired friends who were facing deindexation of their pensions. It is not good enough for the Conservative Government to say the Liberals did it so we can do it too. Surely that is immoral. Fully indexed family allowances are essential if we are to maintain universality as a basic social policy for families. Pensioners understand that. To reduce family allowances by 3 per cent through deindexation is to erode universality. The Minister is shaking his head. Social policy groups which
appeared before our committee have said this and they reiterated it when they opposed the steps he has taken. If this country can afford to subsidize banks and oil companies and increase defence expenditures by billions of dollars, surely we can afford to keep full indexation for family allowances. This Party intends to fight this move as strongly as it can and we will have many speakers before we let this Bill go to committee.
