subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is rather surprising the Progressive Conservatives should have adopted as their strategy not to speak to a Bill that is so important to all Canadian families. Usually, when an important Bill is tabled in the House, once the Minister has made its introductory speech he is followed by the Official Opposition, the third party and then by a Government Member speaking in support of the Bill tabled by the Minister. Today, it seems no one could be found on the Government side who had the courage to support and defend the Government's policy. 1 think I know why.
I know why, because since September 4 last year and especially since this Government was sworn in, we have been faced with a series of contradictions and policy changes that have made things very confusing for us on the Opposition side, and now on the Government side, it stands to reason Members are afraid to rise and support this Bill because they do not know whether they should support what was said in the Progressive Conservative Party's pre-election advertising, the statements made by the Minister of Finance last November or the contents of the Throne Speech, or whether they should support the position taken by the Minister of National Health and Welfare before the Bill was tabled. In fact, Progressive Conservative Members do not know their Government's position. Faced with these serious contradictions, they thought the best they could do was to say nothing. However, Mr. Speaker, that will not prevent us on this side of the House from reminding Canadians what the real impact will be of Bill C-70 on Canadian families.
We want consideration of this Bill to be postponed, to give all Canadians a chance to find out exactly what Bill C-70 will do and to make their views known to this Government, and 1 am sure that as soon as the Canadian people have had time to speak to their elected representatives, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will want to withdraw the Bill without further ado.
September 16, 1985

Mr. Speaker, thinking back to the months that preceded the 1984 election campaign, I remember advertisements that appeared in this country's English and French newspapers, taking a stand against de-indexation. These advertisements, which were paid for by the Progressive Conservative Party, by the present Government, said for instance that the Progressive Conservative Party was against de-indexation of old age security pensions and family allowances. Subsequently, during the election campaign, we heard those famous words spoken by the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party that our social programs were "a sacred trust" that would not be tampered with. Later, Mr. Speaker, in this Government's first official document, the Throne Speech, where the Prime Minister, through the Governor General, announced his Government's intentions, we find that the Government was going to set a priority on strengthening the Canadian family and increasing assistance to families with children.
Mr. Speaker, after all the statements made by Government Members before and after the election, we had a right to expect this Government to introduce a family policy that would increase family benefits and help families in need or on very low incomes and who have children. However, in spite of all the statements and announcements by the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party, they are doing the exact opposite, and the net result of this Bill is that the rich will be richer and the poor will be poorer.
Why introduce a Bill that is so hard on families, at this stage in our country's history? When we look at statistics on demographic trends in this country, we see that the birth rate is falling and that the demographic "pyramid" reflects a definite aging of our population. If only to establish a consistent population policy, I think an entirely different approach was necessary. Aside from the very genuine needs of medium-and low-income families, and looking in purely demographic terms, what this country needs, as the Throne Speech seemed to indicate, is a family policy, a policy to increase the birth rate. What we have here is a policy that is going to have the exact opposite effect on Canadian families, and especially on those with medium or low incomes.
Mr. Speaker, given the thrust of the section and looking at this Bill in the wider context of budgetary policy, we come to the conclusion that Bill C-70 constitutes an insidious and direct attack against middle and low income families. Indeed, an appropriate review of this measure has to be done within the context of the Budget as a whole. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) introduced his Budget last May he made public a number of tables in an attempt to demonstrate-and on many occasions I heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) resort to that argument-that families would stand to benefit since the child tax credit would be increased. That is completely false! I am sure that when the Hon. Member for Gaspe (Mr. Marin) next meets with his constituents he will go to the trouble of telling them that it may be true that the child tax credit will go up. But I hope he will also tell them that the $50 federal tax
Family Allowances Act
exemption will disappear and that, through partial deindexation of income tax, the over-all tax load of middle and low income families will increase. The net result of all this for families in the Gaspe region as well as those in Lac-Saint-Jean, Montreal, Quebec City, and in fact anywhere in Canada, is that they will be directly affected not only by Bill C-70 but by other Budget measures as well which will boost their basic taxes, raise the sales tax and impose new levies on items which had never been taxed before such as medications that people could obtain without prescription. Mr. Speaker, even leaving aside the whole question of the sales tax, I am sure the Hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Blais) will also want to tell his constituents that his Government is about to take hundreds of dollars from families earning as little as $15,000 a year. Right from the beginning the basic theory of this Government was that the bank president was the one to hit because he earns a lot of money. The idea was to take money from the bank president and give it to the needy. Well, Mr. Speaker, now we know how they operate: they can find $1 billion for the bank that collapsed, but they cannot spare a nickel for family allowances. I hope the Hon. Member for Bellechasse will tell everybody that people who earn $80,000 or more a year will not suffer from this measure, quite the contrary, but that the hardest hit will be individuals and families with incomes ranging from $15,000 to $20,000, and there are lots of those in his riding. I hope he will tell them that, beginning in 1990, the child tax credit will be applicable to families with an income of $23,000, not $26,000 as is the case now. Keeping in mind the fact that inflation, although it has gone down, is still hovering at about 3 or 4 per cent, it means that hundreds and hundreds of families will no longer be eligible for the child tax credit. That will be the impact of Bill C-70, that is what we are against and that, Mr. Speaker, is why we ask that consideration of and vote on this Bill be delayed for six months.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, low income families will be hard hit. For instance, in the case of a family with two children where the husband and wife both work for relatively low wages, say $15,000 a year, there is no way one can conclude that the man and woman in the same family who earn $15,000 all told are "knee deep in clover", as the saying goes in the Beauce area. That family, Mr. Speaker, the husband and wife who both work, have two children and earn $15,000 between the two of them, stands to lose $1,844 under this new policy. What does it mean for a family earning $35,000 where the husband and wife both work? Let us say she gets about $15,000 as a secretary and her husband, in technology or some other similar occupation, is paid $20,000. Here again, these are not particularly high wages. These people stand to lose $3,452 annually, if we consider the impact of the child tax credit, changes in exemptions for dependent children and the partial de-indexation of income tax, because after all, Mr. Speaker, what counts is how much money working men and women have left to spend, because if the Government takes with one hand and takes with the other as well-of course they will say they have added to the benefits for family allowances-the purchasing power of a family is going to be restricted, and what the

September 16, 1985
Family Allowances Act
figures show us is that a couple where both man and wife work, with two dependent children, stands to lose $3,452 under this Bill, plus the impact of the Budget on our income tax.
However, if we look at a working couple earning a total of $80,000 per year, we are getting into a higher bracket. Do you know that this couple is going to lose only $1,125, while a couple earning $35,000 will lose $3,400 and the couple earning $15,000 will lose $1,879? This means the real impact of the Bill before the House, together with other budget considerations, will be that the couple whose two salaries total $15,000, with two children, will lose $1,879 per year of their annual income, while a working couple earning a total of $80,000 will lose only $1,125.
I think it is outrageous we should be talking about people losing money, even if they are people who earn $80,000, because throughout the debate prior to the Budget, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) were saying that reforms in social programs would not be aimed at reducing the deficit but that the Government would try to take from the rich to give to the poor. And that is not the case! Everyone is losing money, the couple earning $15,000, the couple earning $35,000 and the couple earning $80,000. Furthermore, the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare gave the House information that does not tally with the contents of the Budget, because in the Budget and the Budget documents, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) informed the House that as a result of its new family allowance policy, the government would be able to save $40 million.
Mr. Speaker, the terms I should use to describe this situation are unparliamentary, and you know why I cannot use them, but everyone knows what I mean.
For instance, when we see that single-parent families, and I am thinking of the woman, the secretary earning $15,000 a year who has two dependent children, who stands to lose $1,844. Mr. Speaker, has this Government no compassion? Are they telling us that our society . .. The Prime Minister said that the Government was bankrupt, that they had no more money, so they had to make spending cuts, and in line with Conservative philosophy, the first area to feel those cuts is social programs.
It seems to me someone-it seems to me you, Mr. Speaker, could explain why they do not have the money to pay family allowances but did manage to find $8 billion to spend between now and 1990 on the oil multinationals, whose cash flow per barrel of crude has increased considerably. They had the money to do that. Someone will have to explain why there is no money to help a woman who is the sole breadwinner, with two dependent children, and why by the time this program is implemented, she will be losing $1,800 per year, and why the Minister of Finance was able to find one billion dollars to bail out the Canadian Commercial Bank. Someone will have to explain to me and to the Canadian taxpayer why, by the time the program is implemented, a woman with two children and earning $15,000 per year will be losing $1,800, while the
Government can afford to spend one half billion dollars on an icebreaker.
To me, the approach taken by the Progressive Conservative Government is socially unjust and economically unacceptable. It is not true that we are living in a society which cannot afford to look after needy families. And I would suggest that, in 1985, a couple with two dependent children and who earns $15,000 a year could hardly be considered a multimillionnaire family. They have a hard time paying for rent, hydro and food, yet the Government will take $1,879 more from them over the coming years. I fail to understand the logic of this Government. Above all, I do not understand why. Why, particularly after the commitments made by this Government to the Canadian people, after the unequivocal remarks of this Prime Minister who kept repeating throughout the election campaign: Social programs are a sacred trust!
We have seen what this Government did about old age security pensions. And I am saying today that if we look at this Bill in the wider context of other Budget measures we find that it is an unacceptable proposal, a socially unfair Bill, a Bill whose impact will be just as devastating as that of partial deindexation of old age security pensions. I would even say that this Bill will propably have harsher consequences because, in the mid and long terms, it will undermine the very fabric of the Canadian family and affect the demographic evolution of this nation. So much so that, in my judgment, we should not take measures which will make it harder still for people or parents with children to make ends meet. Quite the contrary, we should promote or implement a genuine family policy to help couples who have children and who, from now on, will practically be treated like other couples with similar incomes who, for personal reasons, have decided not to have children.
It goes without saying that, from a tax standpoint, doing away with the exemption for dependent children is a sound proposition. That view is shared by a good many social affairs experts. Some of my colleagues and I have had discussions on that subject in the past, but I have always been concerned by one very specific consideration-why? Deindexing family allowances will reduce their impact, just as reducing child tax exemptions will, but as a result our society will soon end up with a situation where a couple earning $35,000 a year is not eligible for Child Tax Credit, while a next door couple earning exactly the same income, but with three or four dependent children, will be treated exactly the same.
This is not what I call a family policy. If we want to solve the problem and eliminate the undesirable effect which the dependent child tax exemptions is creating for high income families, let us not reduce the basic family allowances by deindexing them! Because, in the end ... I should gladly support a Government decision to completly eliminate the dependent child tax exemption, providing it increases proportionally the basic allowances, so that a family earning $35,000, as most Canadian families do, may at least have access to an additional income to compensate the fact that it must support
September 16, 1985

dependent children. As it now stands, the Government is reducing on both counts by lowering the Child Tax Credit to $23,000. Which means that when the Act comes into force, a married couple with dependent children earning $24,000 or $25,000 will be treated practically the same as a childless couple with the same income.
In my opinion, the policy which this Conservative Government has chosen to follow is not at all consistent with the promises it made when it was in the Opposition, and it is even contrary to what it has promised since coming to power. On the economic level, Mr. Speaker, 95 per cent of these transfers made to low and middle income people are spent on consumer goods; I suggest, therefore, that this Bill is bad because it will reduce the total consumer spending of Canadians.
Because I am running out of time, Mr. Speaker, I shall conclude by saying that just as the Budget did, Bill C-70 will make the rich richer and the poor poorer, which seems to be this Government's objective.

I heard his speech and I want to know how ordinary people could have confidence in his position and that of his party. When his party was sitting on the other side, they had the same policy as the government is advocating today. The Liberal Government deindexed the allowances as did the Progressive Conservatives. subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians can have faith in what I said today for a couple of reasons. In the first place, when considering my record as Minister of Finance in another jurisdiction and the position of the government to which I belonged on family allowances, I had decided as a representative of the government not to tax them, because we thought it would be fairer not to give with one hand and take back with the other-
I should like to add also that on several occasions Members of the New Democratic Party have asked that rather insidious question expecting to draw from it some sort of political prestige, but the Member who has just spoken should indicate that this policy was developed under certain circumstances when inflation had reached 12 and 13 per cent and the Government had asked all Canadians, workers, businesses and those who belonged to various segments of the economy to do their share. It had then been decided that for a given period well delineated in the legislation indexation would be limited to 6 and 5 per cent. As evidence that such a policy was well advised, even if it entailed sacrifices for a short period of time, we had the inflation rate which had then reached 11 and 12 per cent brought down to the point that now it is reduced to
Family Allowances Act
about 4 per cent. Those policies as a whole were successful and beneficial to Canadian families.
This is why I say to the Hon. Member who asked the question that he should not confuse apples and oranges. Governments must react to difficult situations, and 1 could give as an example the French Socialist Government, with which the Hon. Member will probably agree as he shares many aspects of its political phisolophy. The French Government had to respond to certain situations in France, to take some action and to implement policies that more conservative Governments throughout the world would have found it difficult to follow. Particular situations must therefore be faced. In my opinion, when the Hon. Member and his colleagues in the New Democratic Party ask such a question, it should be placed in its true context so that the people who listen to us will not be misled.

subtopic: SHOE MANUFACTURER'S REQUEST FOR FIVE-YEAR IMPORT QUOTAS
SHOE MANUFACTURER'S REQUEST FOR FIVE-YEAR IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the textile and footwear industries are responsible for over 2,000 jobs in the constituency of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, and many thousands more across Canada. With only a few weeks left in the present quota allocation and total indecision on the part of the Government of Canada, the footwear industry is in a deep climate of uncertainty. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) over the weekend indicated in an interview that Canadians needed to become more competitive on an international basis. This was the second such attack by the Prime Minister on the workers and the industry. One cannot help but wonder which side he is on.
If the Prime Minister wants us to believe that he is on the side of Canadian workers and industry, let him show us proof by adopting a policy, such as that advocated by the Canadian Shoe Manufacturers Association, of import quotas for five years, and of better policing of imports. This Association has not asked for the moon, Mr. Speaker. Its position is balanced and worthy of consideration. It is my hope that the Canadian Government will afford this industry the much-needed protection that it so richly deserves.

subsubtopic: REINTRODUCTION OF NATIONAL MINE RESCUE COMPETITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, throughout Canada thousands of miners volunteer their time and effort to train for the onerous tasks involved in rescuing their fellows in case of a mining disaster.
Mine rescue teams hone their skills to a high level of competition, the highlight of which is a national competition where top teams from each region compete to decide the national winners.
For several years the National Mine Rescue Competition was held in abeyance, but this year it was reintroduced. It was held last weekend in Glace Bay where the Lingan Phelan Colliery team, ably captained by Mr. Shelly Gouthro, proved its merit by becoming the over-all national champions.
Eight provinces and territories were represented but, unfortunately, Ontario and Quebec were absent. In order to make this a truly national event, our two largest provinces should participate.
Hopefully at the Mines Ministers' conference being held today in Charlottetown it will be decided that a national mine rescue competition will be held on an annual basis and that all mining provinces and territories will take part in this important event.

subsubtopic: REINTRODUCTION OF NATIONAL MINE RESCUE COMPETITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government is following in the tradition of Liberal Governments by reducing the indexation on family allowances. In doing so, the Government is attacking children and families. The Conservatives also are continuing their obvious intention to erode universal social programs, which Canadians consider are a social right.
Canada's children belong to all of us. They are our next generation. They are a rich resource which we must nurture and cherish. We do not want them to grow up into a two-class society of rich and poor. We want to show we care for all children and recognize the responsibility and the costs of parenting. Let us continue to fight for fully indexed family allowances.
I call on all Canadians who care about families to show they care. Write to your Member of Parliament and to your Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). Start petitions. Talk to your neighbours. Talk to the media. Organize and start a national campaign. Show you care for Canada's kids.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACQUISITION OF GULF SERVICE STATIONS
PETRO-CANADA ACQUISITION OF GULF SERVICE STATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in Saskatchewan there is concern over Petro-Canada's purchase of Gulf service stations. Although the acquisition made it possible for a private sector Canadian company to buy Gulf Canada from an American corporation, there is, nonetheless, an understandable concern about the federal Government expanding its role in gas retailing.
It is the time to look at the future of Petro-Canada. Selling Petro-Canada in its entirety is not a realistic alternative. There is an acknowledged need for some degree of government involvement in the oil industry, but the Government should not be competing against small, privately-owned and operated gas stations. Is it the job of your Government to sell gas?
I compliment the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) on her difficult and obviously successful endeavour of making Petro-Canada more financially accountable and responsible. However, I have two concerns. In order that popular well-managed neighbourhood Gulf stations not be closed down with the Petro-Canada acquisition, I ask that the Minister consider all available alternatives, including leaving the Gulf signs in place.
Second, as Petro-Canada enhances its financial position 1 ask that the Minister privatize Petro-Canada's retail gas operations and offer shares to the Canadian public as soon as possible.
September 16, 1985

subtopic: WORLD CUP SOCCER TOURNAMENT-CANADA'S QUALIFYING WIN
WORLD CUP SOCCER TOURNAMENT-CANADA'S QUALIFYING WIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this weekend in St. John's, Newfoundland, Canada's national soccer team defeated the team from Honduras and qualified for the World Cup soccer tournament. I am sure Members on all sides of this House would want to join me in applauding our players and national team coach.
This triumph marks the very first time that Canada has qualified for the 24-nation World Cup, which will take place in Mexico in 1986. For the past 28 years the Canadian soccer team has been working toward this aim. With this impressive victory, a new chapter in the history of Canadian soccer has been opened.
The national team's victory was first and foremost a team effort. All Canadians can be justifiably proud of the skill, the dedication, and the poise displayed by all our players in the international sports arena. Their perseverance and hard work will be an inspiration to our younger athletes engaged in all facets of sports.
It is fitting that we take a brief time out from cheering on the Toronto Blue Jays in their march toward the World Series, to recognize the valiant efforts of our national soccer team in their quest for the World Cup.

subsubtopic: FUTURE OF PRENTICE-HALL COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you can be assured that I am not here to congratulate the Government. In the interests of the entire issue of Canadian culture and the sovereignty of our country, about which we heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) speak so eloquently on CTC last night, the future of one of Canada's leading publishing companies, Prentice-Hall, can be decided by the Government within the next week. A prominent publisher of established Canadian writers and new literary talent, Prentice-Hall, was recently sold to the American conglomerate, Gulf and Western.
Under Section 15 of the Investment Canada Act, the Government can review foreign investments related to Canada's cultural heritage and national identity. Canadians from every corner of the country believe that the potential sale of this company to an American multinational corporation will have disastrous effects upon the Canadian cultural identity.
I call upon the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) to ensure Canadian control of our publishing industry. I implore the Minister and the Prime Minister to veto the sale of Prentice-Hall Canada to American interests. I ask them to assist Canadian companies in purchasing an important contributor to Canada's literary tradition. Let them put their money where their mouth is and ensure the sovereignty of Canada's publishing industry.

subsubtopic: NEED TO COMPLETE AUTOROUTES IN THE OUTAOUAIS AND LAURENT1ANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the constituency of Argenteuil-Papineau which I have the honour to represent in the House of Commons has unique economic development potential because of its geographic location, its infrastructures for industry, trade and tourism, and, most important, because of the development foreseen for the Mirabel airport within the next few years.
However, Mr. Speaker, we do not have an adequate road system. It is somewhat ironical to note that the largest airport in the world is isolated because Highway 13, linking Montreal, Dorval and Mirabel, is not yet finished and Highway 50, linking Ottawa and Mirabel via Papineauville and Lachute, is also incomplete. Mr. Speaker, three socioeconomic conferences, namely those of the Papineau, Argenteuil and Mirabel regional municipalities, are now under way and the first priority at these meetings is the completion of Highways 13 and 50.
Mr. Speaker, the economic participants in my own riding and in neighbouring constituencies have been asking the provincial and federal Governments to complete these highways for 20 years.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) has assured me that the federal Government would cooperate if the Quebec Government were to develop a five-year plan.
Mr. Speaker, I urge my constituents and the various economic participants in the Outaouais and the Laurentians to put pressure on the provincial representatives of their respective regions so that these highways will be completed within the next five years.

subsubtopic: REPORTED ESTABLISHMENT OF CENTRALIZED POLLING SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the "say one thing but do another" style of government continues to roll along. No sooner had the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) boasted that he uses polls less than any other Prime Minister then we learned that the Government has developed a new polling system. The Government will now conduct a massive in-depth poll on a monthly basis. The results will be so secret that even Cabinet Ministers will not be able to know them. Only the Prime Minister and his few henchmen will be able to see the results from which they will plot their strategies.
Of course the taxpayers will foot the bill.
Apparently the former Liberal Government considered a similar centralized polling scheme, but even those old professionals at the trough thought that it was a little too much for
September 16, 1985

the public to stomach. Not this Government, though. It sweetly smiles and says one thing, and the next day it does the exact opposite. George Orwell's doublespeak is alive and well with a Government that will do anything to keep itself in power.
I just hope the Prime Minister will learn from his private polls that Canadians are tired of Governments which manipulate and mislead. Canadians want an honest Government with a clear idea of what it is doing and where it wants the country to go.

The legal counsel for the Department of Finance asked if I would complete all the legal work required for the possible closing of the bank, to be kept in escrow pending the resolution of the discussions.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the sixth report of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry is a landmark report. The committee unanimously agreed to support a proposal put forward by all the mayors of Vancouver Island. The proposal is a proper and important matter for consideration by this House at the earliest possible time because Vancouver Island has been devastated by the recent recession. The forest industry on the island has undergone some very serious deterioration and it is my hope that the Government would support the proposal put forward by the standing committee.
The riding of the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Schellenberg), who has been supportive of this proposal, is the best example of the effect the recession, as well as poor forestry practices and general neglect, has had on the island. A number of years ago the community of Port Alberni boasted the highest per capital income in Canada. Some of the best employment in this country was in the forest industry in Port Alberni. As time went by and the resource was neglected, as the forest industry failed to keep pace with technological improvements and failed to exploit international markets and essentially turned a blind eye along with everyone else to the resource base in the area, those jobs began to disappear. I understand that about 2,000 jobs have now been lost in that area out of a work force of approximately 6,000 people. As one of the Government's spokesman on this particular Bill, it would be my hope that the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni will stand in his place today and support this motion to endorse the mayors' proposal.
The constituency that I represent covers about one-half of Vancouver Island. If a line were drawn across the centre of the Island we would be looking at one-half the total area of the island. Within the riding of Comox-Powell River there is an enormous dependence on the forest industry. Over the years we have seen a tremendous downgrading of the operations of that industry. Communities such as Courtenay, Campbell River, and many other small communities now require, regrettably, the presence of soup kitchens. This kind of operation was developed in response to the erosion of the employment base on the island, particularly the collapse of the forest industry and the forest resource. The mayors of Vancouver Island are asking the federal Government to recognize that it has an obligation to the people of Vancouver Island to assist in restructuring the resource. The federal Government has a responsibility for job creation. It has a responsibility to protect the resource from which it derives a large amount of income
Committee Reports
and sales taxes. The federal Government has been a tremendous beneficiary of the wealth generated from that resource but it has unfortunately failed to fulfil its responsibilities to the communities there in restoring the forest base. In my opinion and that of my colleagues on the committee, the mayors' proposal would mean only a modest contribution in order to bring about the improvement in the forest base which would restore the resource to help bring employment on the island back up to its previous level. It would provide people with the opportunity to earn decent wages in a very meaningful activity which would produce wealth in the short term and improve the resource for the long term.
It is important that the federal Government and the Province of British Columbia have concluded an Economic Regional Development Agreement through which $300 million will be spent for reforestation. Unfortunately, no significant amount of that investment will be spent on Vancouver Island but, instead, will be spent in other areas. The other important aspect of the ERDA agreement is that professional organizations within the forest industry, such as forest research organizations and the School of Forestry at UBC, are of the opinion that this amount of money is infinitesimally small considering the task of regenerating the resource within British Columbia and particularly on Vancouver Island. The amount of $600 million is required. It would be a serious error to use the ERDA funds, which have already been earmarked for important priority projects. When this committee forwarded its unanimous recommendation its opinion was that the federal Government should be involved in separately funding the proposal of the mayors of Vancouver Island. I urge my colleagues in the House of Commons to support this motion, to concur in the report of the standing committee, and to urge the federal Government to make funds available which are supplementary to the $300 million allocated for reforestation in the ERDA agreement.
The impact of the collapse of the forest industry has been extremely serious on Vancouver Island. There is not a community on that island which has not experienced an enormous negative effect due to the loss of employment created by the downsizing of the forest industry. The Macdonald Commission said that forestry was a sunset industry in Canada. Nothing could be further from the truth. The forest industry has a long and viable future based on a sustained yield resource. In perpetuity this country can derive its wealth from the forest industry. It would be a serous mistake for the Government to ignore that. We have stood by and watched that resource being depleted without any concern for reforestation or preservation of the resource on a sustained yield basis.
It is important to note that forestry, in a depressed region such as Vancouver Island, is the quickest and most effective way of developing income and employment. It is extremely important that the Government realize that many of the long-term projects which have been conceived for that area may produce employment and economic development in five to ten years. However, an investment of the magnitude proposed

September 16, 1985
Committee Reports
by the mayors of Vancouver Island would almost instantaneously create substantial employment and substantial improvements to local economies on that island. To my knowledge, and that of many others, there is no more effective a mechanism for the quick generation of employment in a severely depressed area. There is no more worth-while an investment of federal tax dollars than in the regeneration of a resource which, with sustained yield management, on-going reforestation, and intelligent forest management practices, will yield perpetual wealth and employment and a strong economic base for the people of Vancouver Island in the future.
The reason for debating this issue in the House today is that this was proposed about a year ago. Mayors of Vancouver Island have been coming to Ottawa to visit Cabinet Ministers and talk to Conservative Members of Parliament. Everyone agrees that this is a great idea and they all support it. However, in spite of their election promises and individual commitments, no one on that side of the House is willing to make the move by writing the cheque for the amount of money required to fund this proposal.
It is critical that before the House adjourns this afternoon we vote on the issue of contributing a substantial amount of money on an on-going basis to the forest proposals of Vancouver Island. This concept is endorsed by the federal caucus of the New Democratic Party in Ottawa, the provincial New Democratic MLAs, and even by the Social Credit Party which usually has trouble seeing common sense in any issue. The Liberal Party has also endorsed this proposal as has the Conservative Party in Ottawa. Therefore, it is absolutely incumbent upon the federal Government to produce the funds very quickly to begin the process of revitalizing the economy of Vancouver Island.
The official unemployment rate on Vancouver Island is 15 per cent which is among the highest in the country. However, the real unemployment rate on Vancouver Island is much higher. Many people realize that there are no jobs available and that there is no purpose in going to the employment office to apply for work. In many communities the actual unemployment rate exceeds 25 per cent. This applies not only to Vancouver Island, but to the sunshine coast, the Gibsons area and the Sechelt area, a population of approximately 12,000 people who have experienced a severe economic recession. They have seen the forest industry, once the prime generator of wealth in that area, collapse.
The Mayor of Powell River has been attempting diligently to develop a program which would mesh with the Vancouver Island municipalities. Powell River is a member of the Association of Vancouver Island Municipalities which has backed this proposal. It is important that that regional district be included in the proposal of Vancouver mayors for funding for forestry.
1 see that the Member for Nanaimo-Alberni is now in the House. I am certain that he will be rising to speak in support of this proposal as the communities of his riding are dependent on forestry. MacMillan Bloedel, the single large employer in Powell River, a region of approximately 20,000 people suddenly laid off 500 people. Once you have lost your job in the major operation in such an isolated area you can usually no longer afford to live in the community. Housing costs, transportation costs and the cost of food and other necessities in that community are very high. When a major employer lays off 500 people in such a community, no one will purchase homes there. Housing prices tumble, unemployment is persistent and chronic. Those who have lost their jobs are essentially trapped in that community, cursed with the prospect of long-term, chronic unemployment. Not only does this cause problems within the community, the local economy will implode in many respects. As a result of those 500 lay-offs, many local businesses will not survive, with the result of even further employment losses and a continued imploding of the economy. I would compare the effects on Powell River to those suffered by Port Alberni over the years with the down-sizing of the forest industry there.
Among the many other proposals to improve the economy of Vancouver Island, the federal Government should seriously consider the tourist promotion that accompanies Expo '86. The people of Vancouver Island fear that they will not be able to share in the benefits from the money which the federal and provincial governments are putting into Expo '86 that will attract people to Vancouver and the area. It is estimated that some 13 million people wil be attracted, but they will certainly not go to the communities of North Vancouver Island.
Approximately 80,000 people live in that area. Unfortunately, rather than attracting tourists to that area, Expo '86 will attract many people from Vancouver Island-those who are employed and can do so-and each family will remove hundreds of dollars from those island communities to spend in Vancouver. In fact, the local economy of those communities on Vancouver Island will suffer because of the investment in Expo '86.
While Vancouver and the major metropolitan areas will benefit, I suggest there will be a net loss on Vancouver Island as a result of the federal and provincial tax moneys spent and the enormous volume of money removed from the island. I belive that by the winter of 1986 there will be a shortage of cash on Vancouver Island and a reduction in spending in those communities as well as a general deterioration of the economy for some time.
If the federal Government will make such a large investment in Vancouver, I believe that investment will be seen as having a net negative effect on Vancouver Island and, coupled with the already depressed economy, it is incumbent upon the Government in the name of equity and fairness to make an investment on Vancouver Island to improve that economy.
Clearly, if the federal Government is interested in creating employment on Vancouver Island, stimulating the local economy to restore small businesses and rehiring those young people who are trapped and essentially without hope, an improved forest industry, reforestation and silviculture programs are the most effective and efficient way of doing so. In the face of
September 16, 1985

those difficulties, I expect that the Government would be prepared to support such an initiative. These communities are simply asking for an annual investment of $22.5 million. I see that you are signalling me to resume my place.
Finally, I urge my colleagues in the Conservative Party to support this effort. It is an enormously exciting proposal which they should support today.

However, I have rushed here to speak on this issue because it is so important to my riding. I say that somewhat tongue in cheek because I am far from dead on this issue.
I want to thank the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell (Mr. Skelly) for suddenly raising this issue and showing sudden interest in the Vancouver Island mayors' proposal in their strategy for survival.
I believe it is important to review the history of this strategy for survival. My office was contacted last fall, when this was initially proposed by the Mayor of North Cowichan and his colleague, the Hon. Graham Bruce. We were able to arrange transportation for the Mayor and his committee to Ottawa. As you know, Mr. Speaker, being a former Member of Parliament yourself-

I am sure that you are aware of the work involved in making sure that the doors in Ottawa are opened to delegations from ridings and ensuring that these people have access to the corridors of power in Ottawa.
On many occasions opposition Members were unable to do so and your humble servant was able to arrange these contacts between Members and Ministers, especially the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew). A meeting at my office was arranged so that this kind of proposal could receive the attention it deserves.
Next, several times I attempted to raise this issue at the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, but it was delayed by opposition Members who believed that the fisheries Bill at the time was of paramount importance. Therefore, I am rather surprised to see these sudden born again foresters in the
Committee Reports
opposition Party who are determined to have this issue go through the House today.
Let us consider what the Government has done for forestry since the election in 1984, because I believe it provides an important background when studying this issue. During the election campaign we promised that there would be a Minister of Forests.
That is an important first step in giving Canada's number one employer the attention it deserves. Second, there is the agreement to which I was very proud to contribute. It is the Economic Regional Development Agreement for British Columbia, involving some $575 million, $300 million of which went directly into reforestation programs in British Columbia. That is five or six times more than what the previous Government deigned to give the Province of British Columbia on forestry, but I believe it shows the new kind of emphasis that our Government is giving this particular aspect of the Canadian economy.
Another specific incident which perhaps demonstrates our Government's emphasis on the forest industry happened at the time when the central Vancouver Island area was faced with the loss of some 250 Employment Bridging Assistance Program jobs.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss Macdonald) met with individuals whom we brought to Ottawa from my riding and rescued those jobs with some $1.2 million being put back into the program. This occurred some two months after the province had withdrawn its support for that program.
With respect to the countervailing duties argument, there is a growing protectionist and isolationist sentiment in the United States that is threatening our British Columbia forest industry. Our Government is not ignoring this issue.
This summer we sent an all-Party delegation to Washington, D.C. to discuss the issue with the American Senators and Congressmen. On August 2, in Vancouver, B.C., we met the Minister of Trade, the Forestry Minister, Members of Parliament including Opposition Members and Stan Gibbons, the Congressman who is pushing this Bill through the U.S. Congress. Those discussions continue, which shows the emphasis our Government is putting on the forestry issue.
I must take exception to the comments last week of the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton). He said that our Government is not paying this issue the attention it deserves. As I stated in the House on Friday, it is time that the New Democratic Party learned who its friends are. Valid criticism is warranted, of course. But the U.S. Government is our friend. The United States of America is our greatest market-place. We need the Americans for our B.C. forest products. You certainly cannot go around deriding the American Government on the one hand and asking it on the other to buy B.C. forest products. That is talking out of both sides of your mouth. If you keep on doing that, people stop listening.

September 16, 1985
Committee Reports
I think our new Progressive Conservative Government is giving the forest industry in Canada the attention it deserves, and will continue to do so as our mandates over the next 20 to 25 years progress.
I was interested in a comment made by the Members for Comox-Powell River during his speech. He said that it is the obligation of the federal Government to spend money on the resource. This is true. It is also the obligation of the forestry industry to spend money on the resource and to reforest whenever possible. It is not 100 per cent the obligation of the Government of Canada to spend money on the forest resource. One has to remember that.
Let us deal specifically with the Strategy for Survival from the Vancouver Island mayors. It is my hope this program will progress and that it will be funded in part by the Government of Canada. I know the Ministers involved, the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Minister of State for Forestry are very supportive of that program.
In travelling through the riding this summer I found there was one aspect of the program that was of concern to the unemployed foresters. It is not simply a UIC top-up program. I am sure my colleague, the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River will agree that if this program is to progress, there has to be an opportunity for those foresters who have fallen off the UIC program on to the welfare rolls to take part in it also. I hope that is a vital part of the Vancouver Island mayors Strategy for Survival.
For the record, if I may, Mr. Speaker, let me read the immediate response of the Minister of Immigration to our committee's motion of late June. She said that it was an ambitious plan which would require significant financial commitment over a very long period, well into the next century. She said: "Clearly, we are not in a position to support the entire scope of the proposal. However, it is possible we may be able to help through training or retraining mechanisms in support of the development of the workforce. I have recommended that the mayors of Vancouver Island work with my regional officials, who have been involved with the forest investment steering team, to discuss possible ways in which the requirements associated with the proposed activities under the strategy for survival might be met through support under the Canadian jobs strategy."
The Minister of Immigration and the Minister of Forestry have been paying the attention this motion deserves. In fact, they have been paying it a great deal of attention. Finally, before I get to 103 degrees, Mr. Speaker, let me underline one statement in the motion that came from our Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry. It reads:
Your committee recommends that the Government consider the advisability of funding this proposal.
Our Government must look into the viability of funding this proposal, and that is what we are doing. I talked to the office of the Minister of Employment and Immigration this morning. The project is very much alive and will be coming through in the fall. Let me say that that is through the initiatives of the
Members of Parliament on the Government and on the Opposition side, not one or the other.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in my place today as forestry critic for the Liberal Party to indicate our support for the efforts and proposals of the mayors of Vancouver Island. Indeed, as some of my colleagues indicated a few moments ago when I was out of the House, I did not realize that this matter was coming before the House today. A motion was moved, adopted and unanimously approved in committee supporting the efforts of those mayors. That proposal is important because it provides the area of Vancouver Island, or that part of British Columbia, with an opportunity to stimulate the economy and because it provides an opportunity to stimulate the economy and because it provides an opportunity for employment for people in that part of the country. More important, the proposal of the mayors of Vancouver Island can be a real pilot project. It can be the map or the new course which charts the way to renewal of our forestry industry. It deals in a tangible way with much of the unemployment affecting rural parts of the nation from coast to coast. As the forestry critic for the Liberal Party and as a Member of Parliament from the riding of Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe which was a sizeable forestry industry, with two mills and a good chunk of the population working in that industry, I support the proposal of the mayors of Vancouver Island.
I have some concern with those who suggest that the Government of Canada has to be careful not to provide direct assistance to the proposal of the mayors if it will be seen as a subsidy by the American administration and therefore seen as evidence or more reason to move on the threat of countervailing tariffs in the softwood lumber industry. I have real concern that that kind of argument can be made in the House or that we as Canadians have to be careful not to assist our unemployed, or not to rejuvenate our single greatest resource, because we may offend the Americans and give them a case for bringing in a countervailing tariff against that industry. Such a suggestion is tantamount to saying that domestic policy in Canada will be set by an administration south of the border. Such a statement is tantamount to saying that the unemployment in Canada will have to wait until those south of the border are less nervous about the success of our industry in their market-place. Such a statement is tantamount to saying that Canada should neglect its forest resource by allowing continuing over-cutting and an insufficient restocking of forest lands until our friends south of the border are no longer nervous, until the congressional elections are over.
In a sovereign nation which is governed by a democratic institution and operates under a parliamentary democracy, we should not allow ourlelves to make policy on the basis of what is acceptable to an administration south of the border. Surely we are not telling those people who make a living from the forestry resource that we know they need help, we know they

are in trouble, we know that their circumstances are desperate, but they should not bother us right now because Uncle Sam is looking over our shoulder. Our forestry industry is greater in terms of the balance of trade than agriculture, mining, oil, gas and the fishery combined.

That is true, that is a fact. Surely we are not saying that that resource should be put on hold until a new Shamrock Summit can be held and we can sing the same song again as far as trade is concerned.
The mayors of Vancouver Island have done what perhaps Governments at every level have failed to do. They have had the courage, wisdom and initiative not to complain about their plight but to make a concrete proposal to put people back to work to ensure the basis of the economy of their region and to reinvest in our greatest resource, the forestry sector.
Currently we are cutting 700,000 hectares more of forest land per year than we are planting. Every year we are falling behind by 700,000 hectares. Of course this does not take into account great forest fire years like this year in the Provinces of British Columbia where hundreds of thousands of hectares of forest land were lost. Also there are hundreds of thousands of hectares which have been clear cut and where replanting has not been done.
One of the dilemmas of the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) is that he does not have any direct jurisdiction. Jurisdiction in the forestry sector is exclusively that of the provinces. The Minister of State for Forestry has a difficult time. He does not have a stick and he does not have a carrot. He can only express his concern. He can only say that there is a disaster in the making and that if we continue going the way in which we have been going, we will cut off our nose to spite our face. He can only make projections that Canada will lose its place in the international market-place in this industry if we do not act now. However, he cannot act now because the forestry sector is the exclusive jurisdiction of provincial Governments. There is only one thing he can do. He can provide the dollars. If the provincial Governments cannot find it within themselves to make forestry a priority, he can provide the dollars to third parties like the mayors of Vancouver Island. He can provide the dollars for a project which would, as we would say in Newfoundland, chart a new course and fasten a new sail for an industry which is in deep trouble.
The real tragedy of the Canadian forestry industry, even though it is the single most important industry, is that Canadians only know about the forestry what they see on television and hear from Smokey the Bear. The forestry industry takes place out of sight and away from major urban centres. Most Canadians have no idea what is going on in that industry. They drive down the highways and see an endless skyline of trees and they say: "There are lots of trees; Canada has an endless supply of trees; everywhere we look there are forests". They cannot see that beyond the highways and beyond the lands lying in front of them and over the bluff are thousands of hectares of clear-cut forest lands which have not been replanted. They cannot see the trees lying broken and uncollected. They cannot see the stumps rotting in the ground with nothing to replace them. They cannot see the thousands of miles of wilderness land, where animals once roamed and were king, where trees once grew and rivers flowed, dead and dormant. They cannot see the problems of the forestry industry in Canada, the so-called land of great forests and wilderness, the so-called recipient of God's great gift of the forest. Unless we intervene dramatically, the industry will remain in trouble.
If common sense prevails in Parliament and if non-partisanship can rear its rare head, we will support this motion of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, in the interest of seeing trees planted which will not even be ripe for harvest for 40 years or perhaps when many of us are no longer on the face of the earth. We should all support this motion. We should ensure that before five o'clock it passes by way of vote. In fact, we will do it right away. We will support the efforts of the Conservative Member from Vancouver Island who wants to see some assistance for his region. Members of Parliament like myself from areas suffering 30 per cent unemployment are prepared to see a substantial amount of money going to an area with a much better employment picture because it is a pilot project which will show our areas the way. I hope we can move concurrence in this motion today. I hope we can come to a quick vote and that our commitment to future generations will prevail over our short-term partisan political considerations.

Mr. Speaker, I am particularly pleased with this opportunity to address the problems of the forestry industry, since two thirds of the economy of my riding and the general area depends on that industry and its products. The issue is a very important one to us. We do not happen to be in British Columbia, but just the same, the forestry industry in Eastern Canada is very important to us. In fact, the largest municipalities in my riding were created thanks to the forestry industry. The Municipality of Gatineau
Committee Reports
owes its existence to CIP, and the City of Buckingham to Maclaren, and the same applies to Thurso. This issue is therefore important to us.
Mr. Speaker, during the election campaign, I was among those who asked for a Department of Forestry, not just to have one more Minister but because this sector is vital to my region and to the entire country. In fact, I hope the Department will set up its offices in our region so that at last our eastern forests, the forests of Central Canada and especially our hardwood forests which are seriously threatened, will have a spokesperson with an interest in their future.
What major issues would the Department have to deal with right away? Any one would agree that reforestation should be at the top of the list. Fortunately, one of the new Department's first steps was to sign a federal-provincial agreement with Quebec and the other provinces to set up a forest conservation, renewal and reforestation program.
In my riding, these are very real concerns because of the present crisis in the forestry industry. Because plants must go farther and farther afield to get their raw materials, their wood supply has become increasingly expensive. Some of the smaller sawmills, for instance, have been forced to close because the cost of wood has become so prohibitive they can no longer continue to operate and compete with the US and especially with new markets in the southern hemisphere where forests mature more rapidly because of the warmer climate. 1 therefore hope that thanks to this agreement between the federal Government and the provinces, we will be able to ensure the reforestation of our forests and the wood supply our plants require.
In my riding, the Maclaren Company, for instance, a family operation that now belongs to a large corporation, has finally established its own nursery in our region. Mr. Speaker, that tree nursery is using new seeding and growing methods and they also have new training programs for youths because it is a sector where many of them can find employment.
I therefore hope that we will maintain our efforts in an attempt to reach a federal-provincial agreement under which we might consider the possibility of joint university training, the kind of program enabling young Canadians to spend a few months working for a paper company or in a tree nursery and then perhaps go on to complete their course in a university during the other months of the year. A great many of those young people come from very poor families in our region and simply cannot afford to quit working to take university courses, but they can see for themselves that the preliminary or technical elementary level does not offer employment prospects and good pay in a highly competitive world. It is therefore a matter of renewing supply, renewing training and forestry technique.

September 16, 1985
Committee Reports
On top of that, Mr. Speaker, we do have a lot of ground to cover in terms of staff training. I am quite pleased to hear that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) has been successful in reaching an agreement with her provincial colleague with respect to vocational training and that they are both looking at ways of providing the kind of industrial training which will not cut into the traditional provincial field of education.
You know, Mr. Speaker, it is very imperative that we get on with such on-the-job training. In my riding, for example, the large CIP company wants to replace one of its machine by a new one which can compete with developing countries, especially southern countries which, as I pointed out, can indeed find new and cheaper supplies. To do that the company will have to retrain a great many of its employees who work in the paper mill.
So, Mr. Speaker, we must put the emphasis on staff training on the job, and that is why I am pleased that the new programs of our Minister of Employment and Immigration will enable us to do just that in the near future.
And yet, Mr. Speaker, there is another question which is even more relevant than the first two, however important these may be, and it is the question of diversifying our forest products. In the course of discussions at our Outaouais socioeconomic summit we found out that a silvichemistry centre in the Outaouais would be a good example for the rest of the province and provide advantages and new markets which are unavailable right now. That is why I am very glad to see that all participants at the socio-economic summit and all spokesmen for the steering committee who come from every community in the region and from various quarters have agreed to give tcp priority to a silvichemistry centre.
What does silvichemistry mean to us? It means that we can use the discards of a paper mill, it even means that we can develop new methods, new clean energy sources for our cities, our homes and our institutions.
Mr. Speaker, this even means discovering new drugs, which might surprise some people, but residues from pulp and paper plants can be used to make drugs to fight respiratory ailments such as those which are resistant to antibiotics.
Mr. Speaker, we therefore have a whole new industry in forest resources.
To achieve these results, we need the cooperation of all levels of Government. We also have to set our priorities.
When we want to provide assistance to a plant or a sawmill in our region or constituency, we might find that somewhere else in Canada, in another province, there is a surplus of the same product or raw material.
Mr. Speaker, being a national Government, we face the dilemma of developing the regions, especially if they are dependent on forest resources, while governing the country
responsibly by guaranteeing that jobs will not be moved from one part of the country to another. The forest industry provides a perfect example of this dilemma.
I have myself occasionally requested subsidies to help sawmills or small paper plants and been told: If we help your region, we shall create unemployment in British Columbia or New Brunswick.
Mr. Speaker, we can obviously not implement a forestry policy without devising a new approach to regional development. This is why I am very happy that our party is seriously considering a new regional development policy and that our Quebec caucus, for instance, of which I am a member, has created a sub-committee which will focus on a new approach to regional development, especially in sectors such as the forest industry, which are threatened by supply imbalances throughout the country.
Mr. Speaker, we have discussed a regional development fund under which regional priorities could be identified without harming the national policy which must be implemented.
When discussing the forest industry in the perspective adopted by the Hon. Member, who has moved a very specific motion, we have to remember that, while he emphasizes the importance of a solution, if the Government does not approach the planning of national policies seriously, it could create as many problems in the rest of the country as it would solve in his own region.
It is therefore not because of some reluctancy or lack of courage on our part that we want to examine seriously a national forestry policy with a regional development orientation, but because our country is made up of different regions.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my colleagues from British Columbia, who must naturally deal urgently with their own problems, not to forget that our country is made up of regions, that its diversity is also its strength, but that this diversity creates rather special problems when we are trying to develop a national policy in any given area.
Mr. Speaker, I would therefore ask them not to try to be too controversial in this area because thousands of jobs are involved, the future of our country depends on it and the forest industry remains one of the major sectors of our economy.
I would also ask them to cooperate with us in trying to find new markets for this traditional Canadian industry. I am thinking also of the remote sensing system which we have finally adopted in this country. Mr. Speaker, this system makes it possible for us to carry out an inventory of our forests through satellite slewing, so that instead of being satisfied with a rough survey made on site, we can now have a global picture of our forests, we can supervise their growth and health, as well as plan their development and protection.

Mr. Speaker, I call on my colleagues to closely cooperate in the area of forestry, because a great many jobs depend upon it and also, somewhat, the pride of our country.
