speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to have an opportunity to participate in the debate with respect to the motion for concurrence which is before us. The recommendation which we are dealing with here, which is the Vancouver Island mayors' proposal, Strategy for Survival, is an important one. Many people on Vancouver Island, and in British Columbia, will read this afternoon's proceedings. It is important that as they read it they understand what the procedure being followed here is. That is to say, the Govenment has an opportunity this afternoon, before five o'clock, to allow the motion for concurrence to come to a vote. If the matter does not come to a vote, then it is put on to Government Orders where it can remained buried for months and months, as happened with one of our previous motions concerning CN twin tracking. We need to come to the brass tacks of the issue, since it is clear that Conservative, Liberal and New Democratic Party members who sit on the committee voted in favour of the Vancouver Island mayors' proposal. It is a very well put together and researched proposal. It could well act as a planning model which could be applied to other areas of British Columbia, to those areas of the prairies provinces with a forest base and to Ontario, Quebec and the Maritimes. It really is a national application. With a few changes it could, in fact, be applied in the Northwest Territories and Yukon.
Government Members, and everyone else, particularly Members from Vancouver Island, cannot continue to send the signal to everyone on Vancouver Island that the cash is about to flow, as the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) makes it seem, while months and months and more months and months are allowed to go by. We have to bite the bullet with respect to this issue. Members of the House should know exactly what the forest investment proposal is for Vancouver Island. It is an investment of $22,350,000 per year in an ongoing Vancouver Island Forest Improvement Program which will create 1,116 permanent productive jobs directly in the forest and a further 500 jobs in indirect employment. Part of the intent of this measure is to attrack back into the forest sector younger workers, with the remaining jobs going to small businesses in the Vancouver Island area. As we have seen in some areas of British Columbia, the average age in some of the

September 16, 1985
Committee Reports
plywood plants is now above age 40. Younger workers do not seem to be finding their way into these traditional type jobs.
The Vancouver Island mayors' proposal is important to this House. I think Hon. Members should tread with care so as not to force this issue to five o'clock just to have it placed on the Order Paper. We should be able to vote on it. Conservative Members of Parliament who sit on the committee agree with me in this respect. They know the problem is in Cabinet with respect to the release of money to British Columbia. It is not a matter of some of the B.C. Tories not being interested in the proposal and supportive of it. It is a matter of breaking the dollars loose from Treasury Board and getting them out to the project. I am sure many Conservative Members would like to see the matter come to a vote this afternoon. I see a great many nodding heads across the floor so I know that, in fact, is the case.
What the implementation of the proposal would do is affect the level of annual investment at the time of harvest, which would be about 45 years down the road. It would increase harvestable volumes by 33 per cent, or 9.5 million cubic metres. It would increase the total value of the harvest by 55 per cent, or $655 million. That is a pretty good investment for the number of dollars we are talking about putting in. Implementation of the measure will increase employment by 33 per cent, or 38,000 jobs. It will increase revenues to Government. I am sure the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), if he is listening, would like to know there is a way in Canada by which revenues can be increased to Government by some 33 per cent, or $79.5 million per year. These revenues will generate, at net present value, a real 6 per cent discount rate of between $4,000 and $6,000 per hectare, depending on the project and site quality, with treatment costs bearing between $200 and $460 per hectare. That is a very nominal investment for a major return.
I have made it clear that members of the committee in a very non-partisan way brought this matter forward in the interests of a part of Canada which is suffering a real decline in one of our primary resource industries. I want to make it clear that we have to let this issue come to a vote today. I do not think that people on Vancouver Island who read the speeches given this afternoon and who suddenly see the matter come to an end at five o'clock when the Speaker announces Private Members' Hour should understand anything other than the fact that the Government talked the issue out in order to put it back on hold.
I would like to tell Hon. Members of some of the problems we are seeing in the forest industry in this country. It is our largest industry and our largest source of balance of trade payments. The B.C.-Ottawa federal forestry ERDA for $300 million for reforestation has just been put into place. It sounds like a great deal of money but, as Les Reid, who holds an independent chair at the University of British Columbia's forestry school pointed out, we should be spending $300 million per year just to deal with the NSR, whereas Jack Walters, a professor of forestry at UBC pointed out, we should be spending $600 million per year if we really intend to deal
with the backlog and the NSR in British Columbia. Let me point out that Sweden gets four times the wealth out of an acre of forest than British Columbia-and that is for comparable acreage-while British Columbia has half the trees in Canada and produces less than half the value in dollars.
Vancouver Island, Mr. Speaker, has a base of over three million hectares. Productivity capacity on even the average growing sites on Vancouver Island are at least four times better than the Canadian average. On Vancouver Island the general levels of unemployment are approaching 15 per cent and in many of the communities, as our witnesses from Vancouver Island pointed out to us, the largest source of dollars in some of those Vancouver Island communities are unemployment insurance, Canada Works and welfare. What kind of a legacy is being left in these declining moments of the forest industry in this country?
In British Columbia one person in five is employed as a result of forest industry activities. One job in the forest industry supports two indirect jobs and one job in logging supports 3.6 jobs in conversion plants, 9.2 jobs in indirect services and 12.8 jobs in total. These statistics might sound bland but they are the underlying foundation of some very sound and careful planning and evaluation which has been done by the Vancouver Island mayors in bringing this proposal before Parliament with the hope, of course, of getting not only federal support but provincial support as well.
The legacy for this country is a bad one at the federal level. For a decade and a half under former Prime Minister Trudeau, less than five cents out of every dollar brought in directly and indirectly through taxation by the forest sector actually went back into any kind of research and development or helped Canada's largest industry. That is less than five cents out of the dollar. There are some industries in this country, Mr. Speaker, which receive very close to a dollar back for every dollar they produce for our economy. The forest sector has been bled heavily by the federal Government and 1 hope that the new Government will look carefully at the fact that it still has yet to increase what goes back into the forest sector beyond that five cents out of every dollar.
One article which I took considerable interest in was written by the dean of forestry at the University of British Columbia, Robert Kennedy, who pointed out a number of things in an article called "Timber-r-r", and I quote:
Forestry is Canada's largest industry, directly employing almost 300,000 people and indirectly responsible for the jobs of another 500,000. One in ten Canadian workers depends on the $23 billion forest industry for a living.
British Columbia in particular is dependent on its trees. Twenty per cent of British Columbians are directly or indirectly employed by the forest industry.
He goes on to say:
In the past 20 years Canada's share of the world forest products market has dropped from over 30 per cent to under 20 per cent.
That is a decline of some 50 per cent.
Brazil and other tropical countries can produce pulp logs in Five to 10 years, compared to 25 to 50 years in Canada. The Scandinavian countries have been
September 16, 1985

practising intensive forest management for 80 years, and now produce three to four times as much wood as Canada per productive unit of forest.
That is three to four times as much, Mr. Speaker. What the Vancouver Island mayors are talking about is mobilizing some of the technologies we have now which are really quite simple. We are talking about conifer release, doing proper thinning, having proper nurseries in place, a proper return on what is called "not satisfactorily restrocked land", and back to full productivity by getting rid of the weeds. There are a lot of things which can be done, many of which are labour intensive, which is good. It gets a lot of people back to work. It is also very good in terms of investment, as I pointed out. For a very small investment we get a massive multibillion dollar return.
The article continues, and I quote:
Kennedy feels we must practise intensive forestry-controlling vegetation, spacing new seedlings properly, pruning, thinning and fertilizing them. If this is done just on B.C.'s good and medium forest sites-25 per cent of the forest land-a substantial gain in forest production will result.
"Practising intensive forestry, you can double the yield of the forest in 45 to 50 years", says Dean Kennedy.
That goes along exactly with what Vancouver Island mayors are saying. There are very few sectors in this country where if you put that small an investment in, you can get that kind of return. I think this House should be looking more carefully at how we can make responsible investments.
I was glad to see the new Government getting rid of the non-productive heavy water plants. I do not believe any Canadians, including people who work there, really felt that the taxpayers of Canada should be putting out over $100 million a year for a product which had no use in Canada. We had no export market for it, yet we made it year after year because a senior Liberal happened to hold the seat. There was no reason for us to continue down that road. We have to start putting money into the productive sectors of the economy where we can put people back to work, get communities back on their feet and generate some revenue, not just for our generation but for a few generations down the road.
I would like to quote Don Whiteley, Sun Business reporter, in his recent article headed "Forest Disaster Looms in 15 Years". He is reporting on Sten Nilsson's report which came out earlier this year. In fact, we dealt with it in our committee. Mr. Whitely said the following, and I quote:
The annual volume of timber available in B.C., now about 75 million cubic metres, will decline to 67 million cubic metres under favorable conditions. Even with productivity improvements, that will mean a five- to 10-per-cent decline in pulp and a five-per-cent drop in lumber. The timber volume could dip as low as 44 million cubic metres, with catastrophic results.
Most plywood plants in B.C. will close by the year 2000 as a result of substitution of other products such as waferboard, which will be produced elsewhere.
A switch from bulk commodity products to greater value-added products is necessary and will help, but distance from markets sharply limits that opportunity, and the industry will be in difficulty regardless.
The industry needs to invest $35 billion by the year 2000 in reforestation and modernization, but "cannot generate sufficient capital... This is perhaps the most serious component in the picture of the B.C. forest industry-it can do little to solve its problems."
When we read a report which is written by an internationally respected economist who tells us these things, we have to
Committee Reports
realize that the money must come from somewhere during this crucial period. I do not believe we should let the industry off the hook. It has been negligent in many of the sites it has operated on for many years. I will be demonstrating that with some statistics in a moment. However, during this crucial period, while we have so many people on Vancouver Island, Prince Rupert, Terrace, Queen Charlotte, Smithers, over to Prince George, down through the Chilcotin, who are concerned, we must try to get this pilot project off the ground so we can apply similar kinds of projects in our own communities. Those same mayors of Vancouver Island have visited my communities and we have similar kinds of pilot projects going. There are a lot of people prepared to go in and work at almost any kind of job which would be proposed.
Mr. Whiteley goes on to say the following in his article:
The amount of timber available to the industry, the report concludes, will be seriously affected even if there is a strong improvement in the economy.
"About five to 15 per cent of the volume is still too expensive to cut, "Nilsson claims. "By 2000, 30 to 40 per cent of the available wood will be too expensive to use due to longer transportation distances, lower wood quality, increased development costs and smaller logs."
There it is in a nutshell, Mr. Speaker. We do not have a lot of options here. The House has to move. We have an industry where less than five cents out of a dollar is being returned to it. We do not find that anywhere else. We do not find it in high tech, agriculture, energy, shipbuilding, textiles, shoes or anything else. There is no other industry in this country which is bled to fiercely by the federal and provincial Governments as the forest sector.
The legacy we are now left with we must deal with. The Vancouver Island mayors have recognized this and all Hon. Members of this House have to recognize it. The summary of the forest and range resource analysis of 1984, produced by the Government of British Columbia, said the following:
-the high-value end of the supply is being depleted ... relaxed utilization standards have aggravated this problem by allowing larger areas to be cut to attain the same timber volume... the long established trend to take the best first has been accelerated. This leaves the lower quality wood to be harvested when the price of forest products increase or when new technology allows cheaper logging and manufacturing.
It goes on to say regarding replanting and silviculture in B.C.:
-the area planted and the number of seedlings planted has almost doubled in the 5 years in B.C.
-between 1979 and 1984 the number of seedlings planted increased from 58 million to 108 million. However, the report states that about 160 million seedlings need to be planted annually.
"Site preparation, brushing, weeding, and present planting levels are insufficient to sustain current levels of annual allowable cut"
Once again we have it in a nutshell. The forest management practices in British Columbia are, to use environmental terms, culpably criminal. Report after report points out that they are harvesting at a rate far faster than it is being regrown naturally or through the little bit of intensive silviculture there is in that province. The Government of British Columbia, in con-

cert with the federal Government, is talcing us down a road to disaster. Look at any serious writer who has written in the last couple of years about what is happening in British Columbia and they all say the same thing: You are over-harvesting. The NSR in the province is larger than the province of Prince Edward Island. That is how big the backlog of sites going the other way is. They are being taken over by weeds, non-commercial species, or they are not growing anything. It is a very serious national problem which we have to deal with in this House.
The summary goes on to say:
-the Ministry's focus presumably was on planting, brushing, and weeding. The report states that "other intensive sivilcultural activites decreased as priorities were shifted to meet increased planting targets"
We see it time after time in the report. The Government is taking the wrong approach. The industry is taking the wrong approach. They are exploiting capital, technology and engineering when we should be revamping our own industry in this country. The report goes on:
-In total NSR land has increased from 1.9 million hectares to 3.6 million hectares (an 85 per cent increase) between 1979 and 1984.
We find that to be very true on Vancouver Island. It continues:
After factoring (i.e. estimating how much of that might actually be stocked upon field inspection), the report states that NSR land has increased from 1.0 million hectares to 1.6 million (a 50 per cent increase in five years).
That is a phenomenal increase, Mr. Speaker. At the same time Ottawa is dribbling out five cents on the dollar and British Columbia is putting almost nothing back into the industry. We should have a national forest act, something I know the Minister responsible supports, and he should be a full member of Cabinet as well as being on the P and P Committee. The Prime Minister should be living up to what he promised in the campaign. British Columbians and people across Canada have recognized that the industry and many provinces have been remiss in this field and we need some federal leadership. I do not think it is wrong, under the Constitution or anything else, for us to be demonstrating that kind of leadership at the federal level. Look at the scientific expertise we can draw on by having Members from all regions of the country and universities and so on in order to get some sound industrial and resource based development going. The report goes on:
-Focusing only on good and medium site land within that total, it has increased from 0.8 million hectares to 1.2 million (a 42 per cent increase in five years). After factoring, the amount of good and medium site NSR land increased from 0.6 million to 0.7 million hectares (a 14 per cent increase).
-Looking at NSR by Forest Region, the most dramatic increase is in the Prince George Forest Region: An increase from 292,400 hectares of good and medium site NSR land in 1979 to 632,700 hectares in 1984 (i.e. an increase of 116 per cent!).
A book was recently written called Cut and Run by Mr. Swift. There is certainly no doubt about that in some areas of British Columbia; the companies, with the full endorsation of Victoria, are going in, cutting the trees down, using them here and exporting them, but they are not doing any kind of serious replanting. When you see an increase in NSR land by 116 per cent, you really know something is wrong.
In the minute that I have left, Mr. Speaker, I would like to reiterate what is going on here this afternoon. We have a motion for concurrence. This House has the opportunity in the next 25 minutes to take a vote on this matter. I am quite confident that my colleagues from the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry will rally support on that side to see that this is passed because it is a Cabinet problem. The Prime Minister and the Cabinet do not want to spend that money in British Columbia. I think we in this House have a responsibility, as British Columbians, Quebecers, Newfoundlanders, even as Yukoners, to get together every once in a while and vote some money for a region which has been so crippled by bad management policies of Government and industry so that this region can have a chance to make a good investment for once. There is a 33 per cent rate of return. You do not get that from the Northland Bank or the Canadian Commercial Bank or the Bank of Mulholland. I think it is about time we started making the kind of resource based investments in silviculture for our young people and start getting this country growing again. So let's get a vote before five o'clock.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HEALTH ADVISABILITY OF INTRODUCING LEGISLATION RESPECTING RIGHTS OF PATIENTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should introduce legislation to ensure, that in communication between physician and patient, a basic human right should include the right of the patient to know one's own state of health and the content of medicines and remedies acquired in drugstores by way of prescriptions.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in developing this motion this afternoon, I would like to illustrate the relationship between the individual who buys a prescription over the counter in a drugstore, the patient and the physician. This is a very complex subject and the time available will not do it justice. The subject is of profound importance to each of us.
When we need a prescription, we want to know and we should know what the prescription contains. That knowledge is such that should be available in detail. In addition, we should know what the side effects are of a particular medicine and what are the counter indications. For instance, when one is taking one drug, and another is prescribed, we should know the effect of it on your well-being, when and how often to take the medication and last, but no least, the purpose of the medication. This right to know does not exist at the present. A patient in his or her relations with the druggist would be much better served if he or she were to have access to complete information and be fully aware of the contents, the effects and the purpose of the medication. Let me repeat that I am talking here of prescription drugs sold over the counter. Drugs that are bought off the shelf have that information. Information, however, is often poorly written, sometimes unclear and often in small print causing difficulties, particularly for our senior citizens.
When it comes to the purchase over the counter of prescription drugs, a lot of work needs to be done. In Canada we have a SIM program, supplementary information medication but it is not mandatory. This program was initiated, I believe in 1981 by the then Minister of National Health and Welfare. The specifics of a medication are explained in detail on a card. It seems the public is little aware of the existence of this supplementary information medication system. The province of British Columbia, however, has a similar system, but for the rest of Canada, it can be safely said that the onus to obtain information about the content of a drug rests with the consumer. The consumer must ask the druggist. The druggist may be very busy, but he will provide the information. What about cases when the druggist provides information that is at conflict with the information given by the physician? Because the onus is presently on the consumer to obtain this information, it is perhaps fair to say that the information is volatile when given in a verbal manner and in competition with other demands imposed on the druggist. Therefore, it is important that this type of information not be left to the consumer but become a mandatory exercise. That is why 1 put this motion on the Order Paper.
We should also ensure that the supplementary information medication system, to which I referred a moment ago, cover all types of prescriptions and provide the fullest information that can be made available at any given time to the consuming public. When we buy corn flakes, the contents are listed on the package. However, when we buy a prescription drug, we do not know what we are getting unless we make a specific request. The information exists somewhere. Why not make this information automatically available to the consumer? After all a person's health is most important.
It seems to me that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) have an important joint responsibility to protect the Canadian consumer who purchases a drug over the counter.
September 16, 1985

1 will conclude this part of my remarks by saying that there are many jurisdictions that require this information be given in a manner readily understood, printed and not left to memory, resulting in a more satisfactory relationship between the consumer of the over the counter prescription and those who provide it.
In the time available to me, I will move on with the other half of the motion before this House, namely the right of the patient to know one's own state of health. I have here a copy of the Code of Ethics published in 1984 by the Canadian Medical Association. I have read the code. It contains a guide to the ethical behaviour of physicians, the responsibilities to the patient, the responsibilities to the profession and the responsibilities to society. It is an excellent booklet, but I was unable to find in it any reference to the right of the patient to know. Why is that? All I have been able to discover in a brief search in an attempt to answer that question was the doctrine of informed consent. I have been told that the Canadian courts are still labouring to qualify the doctrine of informed consent and that the English courts have rejected that doctrine. In Canada it would appear that the expression "informed consent" ought to be replaced with the expression "informed decision-making" or "informed choice" on the part of the patient. Why is that? I submit that it is because it is important that physicians and other health professionals not be induced to believe that they may or should use information simply for the purpose of persuading patients to agree to treatments or to medical goals which professionals have determined to be in the best interest of patients.
As Bernard Dickens wrote in an excellent study on this matter, "the true role of medical information is to serve the autonomy of the patient, permitting the patient to exercise choices which accord to the patient's wishes". Therefore, the patient is enabled to govern himself or herself. At times, as you have probably experienced, Mr. Speaker, the wish of the patient may be in conflict with his or her apparent interest. The two do not always overlap. It is quite true that most people wish that their best interest be served, but when conflict arises between the wish of the patient and the interest of the patient, then I submit that in a free society the patient should be enabled to govern himself or herself by what he or she wishes. Therefore the function of the physician possessing professional or highly specialized knowledge is to provide information which the patient would then consider in order to exercise his or her choice. That is what you would want to do, Mr. Speaker. In doing that, you may decide to proceed in a manner in which your interest and your wish coincide. However, there are many times in certain instances where you may decide to proceed according to your wishes and it may be considered by those surrounding you, including your physician, not to be in your interest. That decision ultimately has to be left in the hands of the patient and, in order to make that decision, the patient has to be informed.
I view of all these considerations and the observations which I have made, it would follow that the right to know of the
Rights of Patients
patient and the imperative necessity of rewriting the code should be discussed in an informed debate of this kind. Of course this will not happen overnight and it will not happen without resistance. However, we know that some physicians will be supportive of the right to know on the part of the patient. In a society which is increasingly so capable and so advanced in its ability to store and distribute information, some physicians will understand that this type of ultimate service of providing information to the patient is not only incumbent upon modern day physicians but is also possible.
Therefore it is important to engage the House in this debate.
I will be very interested in hearing the views of my colleagues on all side of the House. I stressed a few moments ago the rights of the consumer when it comes to the purchase of drugs over the counter. Again I stress that there is an important political role to be played in this instance on the part of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Evidently he would have to give leadership and ensure that we in Canada develop the necessary understanding-politicians, professional people and the public at large-of the profound importance in everyone's life of having the right to full information on the state of one's health, which is the most precious, important and lasting gift given to us as individuals. I leave these points with the House and look forward to what might be a very enlightening debate.

Mr. Speaker, 1 congratulate the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) for placing this motion on the Order Paper and for giving the House an opportunity to examine, even in a very limited way during Private Members' Hour, a subject which is of some concern to many Canadians.
The motion before the House contains two parts. One is that an individual should have the right to know the state of one's health and the other is that an individual should and ought to know the content of any medicines and remedies acquired in drugstores by way of prescription. Both those items are so self-evident that I will not take up too much time of the House debating them. If one visits a medical practitioner, it seems to me that one is entitled to know the exact state of one's health. That is self-evident as well. That is the case with medicines and remedies, particularly prescription drugs. Over the years we have known of numerous cases, thalidomide being one of the worst, I would think, where drugs were prescribed and had a serious adverse effect not only on mothers but also on children. Of course there have been other cases over the years. Everyone who is asked to consume a drug or chemical that alters the state of their being should have the right to know its effect on their health and even on the health of their offspring.
It is for all those reasons, Mr. Speaker, that I think that this motion should properly be referred to the Health, Welfare and Social Affairs Committee of the House so that further discussion can take place. I know full well, as does the Hon. Member for Davenport, and other Hon. Members that much of the

legislation dealing with prescription drugs falls under provincial authority.
However, since many provincial Governments do not seem to be concerning themselves with this, it seems only right and proper that a body such as a standing committee of the House of Commons should make itself available to hear witnesses and to hear concerns not only from individual Canadians but from the health services as well.

Mr. Speaker, on receipt of a request for access to a medical record under the provisions of the Privacy Act managers must seek an opinion as to the presence on the record of any information likely not to be in the patient's best interest. It is the patient's interests and not that of the Department or practitioner that is considered. This opinion may be sought from a duly qualified medical practitioner on staff or from a currently licensed medical practitioner in private practice who also knows the patient.
It is important to emphasize that when withholding of personal information in medical records is being considered, applicants may have the information examined by a practitioner of his or her own choice, providing that the institution is satisfied that the practitioner chosen is qualified to determine whether or not disclosure could be contrary to the applicant's best interests.
The practitioner may advise that the record be released in its entirety, that it be released to the pyisician of the patient's choice for explanation to him or her, that it be made available for the patient to inspect at his or her convenience with a physician at hand to explain it to him or her, or that part or all of the record be withheld in the patient's best interests.
If the advice is to release the record, the manager will either release the record, authorize the privately practising physician to release the record to the patient or return it to the manager for release, ask the patient for the name of his family doctor and if his qualifications are acceptable release the record to him with the suggestion that he explain the record to the patient if he considers it inadvisable to show it, or ask the patient to inspect the record at a time and place convenient for him or her. There seems to be in this particular instance ample opportunity to explore one's own records.
If the advice is to withhold all or part of the record the manager prepares the documents for release with any suggested exempt words or sentences blanked out and in their place
September 16, 1985

the words "withheld by ministerial decision under Section 28 of the Privacy Act". The manager can then send the request, the documents and the reasons for denial of access provided by the medical practitioner to the departmental privacy coordinator for preparation of a letter for the Minister's signature explaining the denied items and notifying the applicant of his or her rights of complaint and appeal.
The process described in the foregoing indicates the seriousness and indeed thoughtfulness with which the Government views its responsibilities to individuals requesting access to personal medical information under the Act. There are, of course, safeguards to protect an individual against harm which might result from the release of information. Although separate data is not available for medical records, experience indicates that there are few situations over-all in which it is necessary to withhold information requested by patients.
It can be concluded that within the jurisdiction assigned to the federal Government under the Constitution, the Privacy Act meets the need for personal access to one's own medical records and no extension of the Act or new legislation is required for this purpose. The Act complements well the ethical and other legislative considerations which influence the practice of medicine which is primarily within provincial jurisdiction. In any case, as I indicated earlier-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) on moving a motion with such a broad social impact.
However, as my colleague said a few minutes ago, communications between physician and patient belong to an area of the practice of medicine that comes under provincial jurisdiction. The provinces have delegated responsibility for regulating the practice of medicine to the provincial colleges of
Rights of Patients
physicians and surgeons or their equivalent, directed by a secretary general. The colleges decide whether a physician is entitled to practise medicine and issue a certificate to that end. They provide guidelines on issues such as patient-physician communications and provide advice to patients. Thus, physicians are advised of their obligations and patients of their rights.
All provincial colleges of physicians and surgeons and all Governments recognize the patient's right to know his state of health. The increased concern of the public in general and special interest groups in particular has brought about a gradual change in public views on patient-physician communications and the scope of such communications. These views have been incorporated in the Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct. The Code of Ethics of the Canadian Medical Association has been adopted by nine provincial colleges of physicians and surgeons, and the tenth Code, that of Quebec, contains similar clauses in its rules on medical practice. The Code of Ethnics of the Canadian Medical Association was recently revised to reflect a change to a more active view of patient-physician relations and the responsibilities of both parties.
The most recent Code of the Canadian Medical Association which goes back to December 1984, prescribes under the heading of Rights of the Patient, that a physician shall:
first, recognize that his knowledge is limited and if necessary, recommend that the patient have recourse to other sources of advice and medical services;
second, respect the right of the patient to choose his own physician and decide whether or not to take the advice given (even after choosing a physician, the patient has the right to ask him to consult other physicians of his choice);
third, respect any confidences received from the patient or a colleague and refrain from disclosing such information without the patient's permission, unless he is obliged under law to do otherwise; when acting on behalf of a third party, he shall ensure that the patient understands his legal responsibility with regard to that third party before proceeding with the examination; and he shall recommend only those diagnostic measures deemed necessary to help him treat the patient and administer to the patient the treatment he believes will be conductive to his well-being (he also has a duty to communicate his observation to the patient and to inform him of his recommendations).
He should supply the patient, with all the information requested by him in order that he may receive any benefit he may be entitled to.
Finally, he should, try and soothe the anxiety of the relatives and work with them in the interest of the patient.
Although the imparting of information to patients by physicians mainly comes under provincial jurisdiction, the Privacy Act provides access to medical information in Federal Govern-

September 16, 1985
Rights of Patients
ment files. This concerns people like natives, Canadian Forces' personnel, war veterans and penitentiary inmates who are looked after partly or totally by the Federal Government. Also, people who have applied for disability pensions under the Canada Pension Plan.
The right to be made aware of one's health status has many facets. There is namely the basic right to know, whatever the reason or qualification. The need to know in order to take steps, make decisions concerning medical care, legal procedures or one's own lifestyle for instance. The right to know what personal data are kept in the various data banks. One of the main requirements imposed upon physicians by provincial colleges of physicians is that they promptly make information available to a third party, where requested by the patient, in order to ensure continuous care, security or the financial arrangements needed. Under the Ontario Health Disciplines Act, Regulation 448 of the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario provides that failure to make available within a reasonable period of time and without reason a report or certificate requested by a patient or his authorized agent concerning a medical examination or care provided is a professional offence. Patients may lodge complaints with the College against physicians who do not comply with that requirement. The College will conduct an investigation and take the required disciplinary action. In Ontario, reports of disciplinary action taken by the College are published each year and distributed to all medical doctors. The limits of acceptable medical conduct is thereby clearly defined, and doctors can amend their behaviour therefrom.
The standard in doctor-patient relations has evolved, from an attitude that could be considered paternalistic to the modern concept of a tacit mutual contract. The latter concept implies that both parties have obligations, and the patient needs sufficient information to make an enlightened decision.
Even though in some cases, by court order for instance, copies of medical Files can be obtained, a physician is generally under no obligation to make the complete file available to a patient or his agent. Pertinent information is generally sufficient, such as results of examinations performed and care provided. A doctor may however give a patient a copy of his file, if he so wishes. Medical files are more or less considered as notes, and therefore the property of the physician rather than of the patient.
Nobody really expects a physician to warn a patient about all the risks inherent in a treatment, only the most obvious and the most serious. However the Supreme Court of Canada has ruled that a physician must warn the patient about the least significant risks involved if the patient wants to know. The physician is guilty of negligence if he fails to do so and if the treatment produces after-effects about which the patient had sought information.
The decision rendered by the Supreme Court of Canada in 1980 in the cases Lepp versus Hopp and Reible versus Hughes
was unequivocal: the patient is entitled to be given information on the state of his health and on the after-effects of a treatment or intervention and the physician is dutybound to provide them. He must give enough information so that the patient can make a sound decision with respect to his treatment. A physician can of course use his own judgment to decide just how much information he should give, but he cannot refuse to give additional information should the patient so request.
In certain cases, for instance in the regulations under the Privacy Act and the regulations of the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Manitoba, safeguards are provided to protect individuals from such information in their file as might be cruel or harmful if it were communicated to them. Here is how Privacy Act Section 28 reads:
The head of a government institution may refuse to disclose any personal information requested under subsection 12(1) that relates to the physical or mental health of the individual who requested it where the examination of the information by the individual would be contrary to the best interests of the individual.
The Manitoba regulations provide that the information given to a patient must contain all the relevant information that he ought to know.
I should like to emphasize the progress made over the past few years which makes it possible for patients to acquaint themselves with personal information contained in their hospital files. The guidelines vary from province to province depending on their respective policies.
The right of access of an individual to information concerning him or her has made remarkable progress. This is true of both medical and general information. These changes stem from a better education of the public, an evolution of attitudes and perceptions, new codes of ethics, as well as new regulations and legislations. Improvements will certainly continue as society is making new progress. In the secrecy of a patient-physician relationship, the patient should expect that his right to know, to ask for and obtain information is respected. It seems that this issue is being dealt with through new legislative guidelines and code of ethics standards. Open discussions and mutual respect are more likely to favour a realization of this objective then a Federal amendment to the Criminal Code.
The practice of medicine, with which the Hon. Member's motion seems to be concerned about, is a provincial responsibility. It is now subject to provincial legislation. This legislation is complemented by the Privacy Act, former Bill C-43, which provides that
-every individual who is a Canadian citizen or a permanent resident within the meaning of the Immigration Act, 1976, has a right to and shall, on request, be given access to
(a)	any personal information about the individual contained in a personal
information bank; and
(b)	any other personal information about the individual under the control of a
government institution with respect to which the individual is able to provide
September 16, 1985

sufficiently specific information on the location of the information as to render
it reasonably retrievable by the government institution.
Mr. Speaker, the present system would appear to be fair and equitable. It promotes co-operation, not repression, and provides for a complaints process to settle any problems that might arise.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin my remarks by addressing the Hon. Member's first point, that is, the right of the patient to know his or her own state of health. It is the position of this Government that, with certain constraints, each Canadian is entitled to information on his or her state of health.
The situation now in this country is, of course, very complex when we start looking into this area. In Canada, the laws governing records such as these cannot be found in any one single place. There are no health records Acts in Canada either at the provincial or federal level. Instead, there are provisions within literally dozens of Acts with respect to patient health records, regulations and, of course, numerous court decisions which are directly involved. Reference has been made to provincial hospital Acts, hospital by-laws, nursing home Acts, public health Acts, occupational health and safety Acts, and even the Narcotic Control Act and regulations made under these various Acts. There have been relatively few court decisions regarding patient records in Canada, at least when compared to the United States, where governmental agencies, both at the federal and state level, have a great number of background cases upon which they can draw. The result of this, of course, is that in Canada the practice of compiling, storing, protecting and ultimately destroying patient health records is largely left in the hands of those who are responsible for gathering it, including government agencies operating various Canadian health insurance programs and other situations.
The primary purpose for collecting and maintaining patient health records is to enable health personnel to treat and care for the patient, in order to reach valid judgments concerning the diagnosis, prognosis and cause of the illness. It also provides a method of ensuring communications between the many different persons involved in the case of a single individual, even within a single institution.
It has been the view of this Government that patients should normally have access to information on their own state of health. However, in most health care institutions, patients do not have physical access to their records and almost certainly would be refused access if they were to ask for it. The argument in support of this position is the generally recognized fact that the patient record comprises a series of entries which serve as a form of communication among various personnel in an institution and as a reminder to those who made those entries. The record is not intended to be a medium of communication from health personnel to the patient. In other words, it is a fairly technical communication. They are usually written in a manner which transmits technical information
Rights of Patients
between specially trained personnel. The entries may, in fact, not be understandable by patients or may be entirely misleading to the untrained individual. For example, routine tests which are undertaken to eliminate the possibility of certain disagnoses within a different diagnostic spectrum may be mistakenly understood by the patient as a form of suspicion or a particular condition, for example, a form of cancer, a venereal disease, or some other disease of that nature.
The points notwithstanding, it is our view that the patient is still entitled to review his or her medical records on the most up-to-date documents that are available in the hospital. We also believe that the patient should receive professional medical assistance, if requested, to enable him or her to interpret the kind of technical information that is contained in the records. I make reference to the use of professional assistance to obviate any misinterpretation which could alarm a patient or interfere with an optimistic approach to treatment and thereby in many cases do more harm than good. This is certainly the case when we are dealing with emotional illness and psychiatric disorders.
We support the right of a patient to this information because his or her treatment, by law, is really solely at the discretion of the patient. Once in possession of this information, the patient will be in a much stronger position to determine whether he or she wants to consent to treatment or to its continuation. I do not need to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that health care is a provincial jurisdiction and that comment thas been made several times today during the debate, and that any changes in federal jurisdiction must be cognizant of provincial responsibilities. At the present time there appears to be no provincial consensus on this issue or on the issue of the right of the patient to view his or her medical records.
A number of provinces, though, have passed legislation giving patients a limited right of access to their treatment records. For example, according to the Alberta Hospital Act a patient does not have a right to his records. The Act is permissive rather than mandatory in its consideration. The law in Alberta allows, but does not require, a hospital board or employee, the provincial Minister of Health, someone authorized by him, or a physician to divulgue patient information. The patient who is denied such information may appeal this decision in a court. The Alberta legislation actually favours the release of information but it places the onus of showing why it should be released on the person who is seeking that sort of information.
The Province of Saskatchewan has a different view. It permits the release of hospital records but has not established an appeal of the procedure to the courts. It does, however, state that the records shall be disclosed upon a court order.
Ontario has a similar regulation for its hospitals, as does the Province of Prince Edward Island. The Hospitals Act of Nova Scotia is similar to the Alberta legislation but allows a refusal on the grounds that "it would not be in the best interests of the

September 16, 1985
Rights of Patients
patient to make available that information". An appeal can then be made to a county court judge.
Quebec, under its act respecting health services and social services, provides patients access to the records in what are known as "establishments" under the Act. These are defined as local community service centres, a hospital centre, a functional rehabilitation centre, a social service centre or a reception centre. A person refused may, under Quebec law, apply to the courts.
In all provinces, special attention is paid to mental health legislation which governs the psychiatric institutions as distinct from the general or public hospitals. There are, of course, obvious reasons for this distinction.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, some Canadian jurisdictions do not have specific legislative provisions or regulations governing patient access to records. Some do, but even those have provisions for only some types of institutions or health care providers and not others. It seems logical and just that Canadians throughout the country should have equal rights with respect to this particular matter. It is equally obvious that uniformity in this respect will require extensive consultation with the provinces, with health associations and with various people involved in the medical industry. Serious consideration must be given to needs, benefits and, of course, risks, because there are a great number of risks involved in the kind of subject we are discussing today.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to direct my attention to the question of the rights of Canadians to know the contents of medicines and remedies which are acquired in any store by way of prescription. This is the second element of the Hon. Member's motion which is before us today. The Government supports the right of mentally competent individuals to know the nature of their drugs. The need to know is greater today, of course, than it has ever been. The fact that modern prescription drugs are far more effective and potent than anything available in the past leads us to expect great benefits when they are prescribed for us, and, of course we expect an instant cure and healing.
No one can argue about the magnificent efficacy of drugs such as poliomyelitis vaccines. We are all aware of the tremendous improvement in cure aids which have accrued to mankind as a result of many of the modern antibiotics. Canadians can never forget the outstanding success of insulin in the treatment of diabetes. We are constantly reminded of significant improvements in the drug control of cardiovascular diseases such as high blood pressure, angina pectoris and the prevention of strokes and heart attacks. These are the good stories, Mr. Speaker. They tell of the beneficial effects of drugs but, unfortunately, as we all know, drugs have a bad side to many of their actions.
Our tendency to emphasize the expected benefits of drug therapy tends to conceal the high incidence of adverse reactions which occur with many drugs. There are in fact no drugs which provide benefits without incurring some risks. We believe that before a patient agrees to take a drug, he or she should be fully advised of the expected benefits of the therapy
as well as the possible toxicities of the medicine. We are too well aware of the stories often heard of patients complaining that they would never have taken one drug or another if they had been told beforehand of its toxic effects. Every one of us has stories and illustrations to demonstrate that. It is the position of this Government, Mr. Speaker, that each patient should be informed of both the beneficial and detrimental effects of a drug before he or she agrees to take it. A well informed Canadian is the best person to decide his or her own drug regimen. I wonder how many Canadians would be dependent on Valium today if they had been told 10 years ago that the continual consumption of this mind-dulling chemical could result in the addiction which has become a bit of a problem for our society.
To this point, Mr. Speaker, I have been discussing only the active ingredients in a drug. I would like now to direct my attention to the so-called "inactive" or "non-medicinal" components in the tablet or liquid. These chemicals are added, as we all know, to assist in the formulation of the product. Without them, tablets would rapidly fall apart, drugs would disintegrate and liquids would taste badly-and my experience with them has been they taste badly anyway. However, these ingredients are necessary to the successful formulation of a product suitable for human consumption. In some circumstances it is these non-medicinal ingredients which are the culprits responsible for toxic effects. Some of these ingredients can induce an allergic type reaction while others can trigger highly undesirable disfunctions of various bodily organs. This very fact creates a problem for the treating physician who is generally not aware of the non-medicinal ingredient of drugs and who may, unwittingly, prescribe an upsetting medication for persons who are sensitive or allergic to a specific chemical substance contained within it.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to review a question 1 asked the then Minister of State for Multiculturalism on May 16, 1985. The question was twofold. It concerned the conference between the federal Minister of Multiculturalism and his provincial counterparts. I
Adjournment Debate
asked the question because Canadians, in particular, minority communities across this land, were anxious to know what this conference would develop.
We on this side were certainly pleased to see this first-ever meeting take place. However, this Government and that Minister created great expectations over this meeting. Every time 1 and other Members of this House rose to ask a question concerning his Ministry, his response was to wait until the conference; wait until May 14 when, for the first time, we will be sitting down around one table and making the decisions which have to be made. Well, we waited until May 14. We waited until May 15. Then, on May 16, the question was asked; Waht were the conclusions?
At the end of that two day conference in Winnipeg, a two-page communique was issued. It was absolutely devoid of any results. There was no mention of the crucial issue flowing from the Abella Report, no mention of the recommendations in the Equality Now! report, or heritage languages, education, human rights, federal-provincial multiculturalism Acts, the Japanese-Canadian redress issue or, last but certainly not least, racism. There was absolutely nothing in that communique to tell Canadians clearly and forcefully what those Ministers discussed and what occurred at that meeting. Therefore, I take this opportunity today and 1 hope the Hon. Member responding for the Government will be able to tell this House and Canadians what has resulted from that meeting on May 14.
The second part of my question was very specific and related to racism. At a press conference following this meeting the then Minister of State for Multiculturalism stated: "Racism really falls outside of our jurisdiction". Mr. Speaker, much to my great surprise these words were uttered following this conference by the then Minister of State for Multiculturalism. It is completely unacceptable for that Minsiter to suggest that fighting racism does not fall within his jurisdiction. First, racism knows no boundaries. It knows no jurisdiction. Secondly, it is the Minister of State for Multiculturalism, beyond any other Minister, who has to fight racism because most of his mandate deals with race relations.
A third criticism aimed at this conference was that it was a closed-door two-day seminar. The communities the conference was supposed to be addressing were not permitted to submit recommendations an agenda, or appear before the Ministers to make their representations. Are we, the Canadian people, the House of Commons, going to be allowed to know what happened behind those closed doors?
If it is the philosophy of the Government that there would be better results if the meeting were held behind closed doors, there is an onus upon it to tell minority groups and all Canadian people what in fact transpired at that conference. Can the Parliamentary Secretary or any other Member clarify what the Minister meant when he said that racism does not fall within his jurisdiction? I see that my time has expired, Mr. COMMONS DEBATES

Adjournment Debate
Speaker, and I look forward to hearing the response of the Government.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique Landry (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to answer the question of my colleague from York West (Mr. Marchi). I think that the steps taken by the Minister of State (Multicul-turalism) (Mr. Jelinek) since we came into office prove beyond a doubt that our Government assumes its responsibilities and is glad to promote this country's cultural heritage.
Among the main objectives of the Minister of State (Mul-ticulturalism), one is to maintain and especially promote equal opportunity for all Canadians, certainly with respect to racism and racial discrimination. The Government fully endorses the basic principle whereby cultural and racial diversity is not only acceptable but advantageous as well. That is why we have been actively promoting the notion of multiculturalism.
This notion entails two major parts, one cultural, the other social. On the one hand, we assume our cultural diversity and heritage. On the other hand, on the social level, we strive for equality among Canadians. While doing so, we must keep in mind those who, because they belong to racial minorities, are faced with various obstacles.
Mr. Speaker, our Government has done a lot to promote progress. It has taken steps to achieve its objective of equality of opportunities for all Canadians. The House of Commons has established a Standing Committee on Multiculturalism. The Federal Government's multiculturalism branch has been raised to the rank of sector.
This Government has undertaken to implement all proposals concerning equity in employment for all visible minorities which ranks, therefore, among the targets, together with women, natives and the handicaped.
The Minister of State soon will make available for wide distribution the United Nations' Action Program for the second Decade in the fight against racism and racial discrimination, in order to better inform Canadians of the various issues at hand.
In view of the tremendous influence of the written and electronic press, he intends to intensify his efforts to encourage the media into establishing voluntary guidelines on the fair representation of visible minorities.
Further, a long-term priority will be the monitoring of the implementation of the recommendations to be found in Equality Now!, which studies many issues raised by the United Nations' Action Program. As we know, a number of these issues span many jurisdictions.
As the Federal Minister responsible for implementing the recommendations in the report, the Minister of State is working with his federal colleagues and having them help him implement those recommendations that come under his jurisdiction. He is also hoping to have the co-operation of his counterparts from the provincial and territory Governments whose mandate covers some of the issues raised in the report.
This Government is committed, as is also the responsibility of the Minister of State (Multiculturalism), to ensure there is no barrier to the full participation of every citizen in the political, social and economic life of this country.

subtopic: FINANCE-DRUG TAX EXEMPTIONS. (B) REQUEST FOR REMOVAL OF ALL DRUG TAXES
FINANCE-DRUG TAX EXEMPTIONS. (B) REQUEST FOR REMOVAL OF ALL DRUG TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, have had an opportunity to challenge the Government for a particular political stance which it has adopted over the past year and which is becoming increasingly embarrassing to the Government. 1 speak of its penchant to blame current Government problems on past Liberal excesses. The billion dollar boo-boo of the bankruptcy of the Canadian Commercial Bank is, according to this Government, the fault of the past Liberal Government.
The illness tax which was imposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his first Budget this May gave us our first chance to see the true Tory colours, the ice-blue blood of the Government. It imposed a 10 per cent tax on hundreds, if not thousands, of drugs that are used on a daily basis by Canadians for illnessess as varied as arthritis, cancer, Parkinson's disease, and heart disease.
Last August when the political heat was on, the Government agreed, through the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), that perhaps it was wrong to impose an illness tax on sufferers of diabetes. When this Party exposed the fact that not only was it taxing diabetics but also taxing those patients with emphysema who needed oxygen, a statement was quickly issued to the effect that certain drugs would be exempted before the House resumed its sitting so that the opposition could not point to the blood and illness tax imposed by the Government.
Therefore, for the public that does not have an opportunity to examine the record of the Government on a daily basis, it seemed as though the problem had been solved. Unfortunately, particularly for those poor people and those families who have to fight illness through over-the-counter medical supplies, the fact is that the Government has left a tax on literally hundreds, if not thousands of drugs.
Let me cite just a few of them for the record so that Canadians will understand that for the first time in our history, the Government has imposed a tax on Pilocarpine which is used by the sufferers of glocoma. It relieves pressure on the eye and if not used blindness results. It is also imposing a tax on Oxsoralen which is used in the fight against skin cancer. Not only is it used for this purpose, it is also considered as an orphan drug, a drug that is not profitable for companies to produce but is produced because of the net benefit to the
September 16, 1985

small number of users who are able to take advantage of it. This is a drug upon which even the drug companies are not benefitting but the Government has seen fit to impose a 10 per cent illness tax. Other examples include Bentylol used in ulcer medication to stop contractions of the stomach and Trihexyphenidyl which is used for the treatment of Parkinson disease.
Most Canadians do not understand the nomenclature ol these drugs, but when they are suffering from arthritis and have to consume copious amounts of aspirin on a daily basis merely to relieve themselves from pain and carry on a normal living they do not expect that kind of expenditure to be taxed by the Government.
Furthermore, when the Government says it will reduce the deficit on the backs of the sick people, that illustrates the kind of mentality which is beginning to become clear to Canadians. That is also a simple economic fallacy.
What about the 10 per cent increase on things like dog food for people who have guide dogs which they use to survive? There are 600 people across the country who need their guide dogs to survive.
If 1 per cent of those people who are now taking over-the-counter drugs decide to go to prescription drugs, since they would be potentially covered under a provincial or private plan, the total amount of savings allegedly derived from tthis particular Budget cutback would be wiped out in one fell swoop.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare will stand up and say that taxes have been imposed by the former Liberal Government. In an examination of literally over 2,000 drugs which are now being taxed as a direct result of this initiative in the Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in May of this year, the Government was able to find four diagnostic tools-not drugs-which had been taxed under a previous tax measure dating back to 1968. It was with this information that the Minister of National Health and Welfare had the gall to stand in his place and suggest that the Government had not only exempted certain taxes imposed by their Government but also had freed up the system from the high taxation measures of the previous Liberal Government.
The kind of double-speak that is apparent in the Canadian Commercial Bank collapse, the kind of double-speak that is apparent in the Minister of National Health and Welfare's response to my direct questions, will not be accepted by the Canadian people.
Do the Canadian people believe that this Government should tax medication being used in cancer treatment, arthritis, Parkinson's disease, and glaucoma? With the literally thousands of dollars in tax imposed as a direct result of the Wilson Budget, this Government is saying it will fight the
Adjournment Debate
deficit on the backs of the sick, the poor, the blind and the elderly. I think it is the kind of political motivation that has shown to Canadians for the first time where this Government's heart really is.
I ask the Government, through the Prime Minister, who refused to answer this question in the House, as well as the Minister of National Health and Welfare, to revoke once and for all this tax which, for the first time in Canadian history, is going to make a profit out of people's illness and potential life-threatening devices.
